questions.q: Which president was the first to be inaugurated in Washington, D.C., in 1801?
questions.explain: Jefferson took the oath at the unfinished Capitol in March 1801 after the election of 1800, the first inauguration held in the new capital.

questions.q: The election of 1800 was thrown into the House of Representatives because of what problem?
options: No candidate ran for vice president
Adams won the popular vote but lost the Senate
Jefferson and Burr tied in electoral votes
questions.explain: Each Democratic-Republican elector cast two votes without distinguishing president from vice president, so Jefferson and Burr tied at 73 and the House had to decide.

questions.q: Which change did the Twelfth Amendment, ratified in 1804, make to the Electoral College?
options: Separate ballots for president and vice president
It ended the role of the House in elections
It gave each state two additional electors
It required electors to be chosen by popular vote
questions.explain: The amendment responded to the 1800 tie by having electors designate their choices for president and vice president on distinct ballots.

questions.q: What principle did Chief Justice John Marshall establish in Marbury v. Madison (1803)?
options: Judicial review of acts of Congress
The right of states to nullify federal law
questions.explain: Marshall ruled that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 conflicted with the Constitution, asserting the Court's power to strike down unconstitutional laws.

questions.q: William Marbury sued in 1803 because he had been denied what?
options: A seat in the House of Representatives
A pardon for a criminal sentence
His commission as a justice of the peace
His appointment as secretary of state
questions.explain: Marbury was a midnight appointee whose commission was not delivered, and Secretary of State James Madison, under Jefferson's orders, withheld it.

questions.q: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from which country?
questions.explain: Napoleon's France sold roughly 828,000 square miles to the United States for about 15 million dollars.

questions.q: Which event most directly prompted Jefferson to seek control of New Orleans and then buy all of Louisiana?
options: Britain's refusal to sell its Canadian territory to the United States
A rebellion by enslaved people in Haiti against Spanish rule
Spain's revocation of the American right of deposit at New Orleans
Spanish troops marching into the Ohio River valley
questions.explain: Western farmers relied on shipping goods down the Mississippi through New Orleans, so losing access threatened the western economy and led to the purchase.

questions.q: Jefferson doubted the Constitution gave him power to buy Louisiana, yet he proceeded. What does this show about his presidency?
options: He believed the president had unlimited treaty powers
He set aside strict principles for national gain
He sought Supreme Court approval first
He acted without any Senate approval
questions.explain: Jefferson favored a limited reading of federal power but accepted a broad exercise of it because the opportunity was too important to lose; the Senate ratified the treaty.

questions.q: Which two men led the Corps of Discovery expedition that began in 1804?
questions.explain: Jefferson sent his secretary Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the Louisiana Purchase and find a route to the Pacific.

questions.q: Which Shoshone woman traveled with Lewis and Clark and helped them interact with Native nations in the West?
questions.explain: Sacagawea joined the expedition with her husband Toussaint Charbonneau and her presence and language skills aided diplomacy.

questions.q: Among the goals Jefferson gave the Lewis and Clark expedition was to do which of the following?
options: Build forts along the Rockies and negotiate removal treaties with Native nations
Map the Pacific coast by sea and found a colony in Oregon
Document nature and Native peoples and find a water route
Locate gold deposits and claim them for the national treasury
questions.explain: Jefferson's instructions emphasized scientific observation, commerce, and a possible water passage across the continent.

questions.q: The Embargo Act of 1807 was meant to pressure which nations?
questions.explain: Jefferson banned American exports hoping to force Britain and France to respect neutral rights, but the measure hurt American merchants more.

questions.q: What was the main economic effect of the Embargo Act of 1807 on the United States?
options: Exports and shipping collapsed, hurting New England merchants
American factories closed because raw cotton could no longer be imported
Federal revenue from tariffs doubled as foreign goods flooded the ports
A new treaty with Britain that opened West Indian markets to American ships
questions.explain: With exports forbidden, ships sat idle and merchants and farmers lost markets, sparking opposition and smuggling.

questions.q: Which British practice angered Americans and helped drive the United States toward war in 1812?
options: Impressment of sailors from American ships
Closure of American ports to French and Spanish goods by Congress
British taxation of American newspapers and legal documents
Seizure of American farmland by British colonial governors
questions.explain: The Royal Navy seized sailors, including some Americans, from US ships, an affront to national sovereignty.

questions.q: The congressional faction known as the War Hawks, led by Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun, mostly came from which regions?
questions.explain: Young southern and western members wanted to defend national honor, end British support for Native resistance, and perhaps take Canada.

questions.q: In June 1812, after President Madison sent Congress a message listing grievances against Britain, what step did Congress take?
options: A treaty of alliance with France against Britain and Spain
A declaration of war against Great Britain
A new embargo closing all American ports to foreign ships
Purchase of Canada from Britain with a cash payment
questions.explain: Congress voted for war, the first time it had formally declared war, in a closely divided vote.

questions.q: Which Shawnee leader built a confederation of Native nations to resist US expansion before and during the War of 1812?
questions.explain: Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa the Prophet organized resistance and allied with the British; Tecumseh died at the Battle of the Thames in 1813.

questions.q: In August 1814 British forces entered Washington, D.C., and did what?
options: Captured President Madison and held him as a hostage in Canada
Marched through Washington peacefully and left government buildings untouched
Burned the Capitol, the White House, and other government buildings
Forced Congress to relocate permanently to Philadelphia
questions.explain: After the Battle of Bladensburg, the British set fire to public buildings in retaliation for the American burning of York in Canada.

questions.q: Which First Lady is remembered for saving the portrait of George Washington as the British approached the White House in 1814?
questions.explain: Dolley Madison arranged for the large Gilbert Stuart portrait to be removed before the building burned.

questions.q: The burning of the Capitol in 1814 destroyed what important collection?
questions.explain: The congressional library, housed in the Capitol, was lost in the fire and had to be rebuilt almost from scratch.

questions.q: After the Library of Congress was burned, Congress rebuilt its collection by buying whose personal books?
questions.explain: Jefferson sold about 6,500 volumes in 1815, forming the core of the restored library.

questions.q: Francis Scott Key wrote the poem that became the national anthem after witnessing the bombardment of which place?
questions.explain: Key watched the British attack on Baltimore's Fort McHenry in September 1814 and saw the American flag still flying at dawn.

questions.q: The Star-Spangled Banner flag that flew over Fort McHenry is preserved in which institution?
options: The Library of Congress in the Jefferson Building
The National Archives Rotunda in the Capitol complex
The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History
The White House Museum in the East Wing
questions.explain: The huge flag, sewn by Mary Pickersgill in 1813, is a centerpiece of the museum's collection.

questions.q: The words of the Star-Spangled Banner were first set to a popular melody from which source?
options: An old French hymn about liberty and the harvest
A British song of a London social club
A Scottish folk ballad about clan warfare
A German march played by Prussian regimental bands
questions.explain: Key's poem was matched to 'To Anacreon in Heaven,' a tune associated with a London gentlemen's club.

questions.q: The Battle of New Orleans in January 1815 made which general a national hero?
questions.explain: Jackson's forces defeated a British assault, even though the Treaty of Ghent had already been signed in December 1814.

questions.q: The Treaty of Ghent that ended the War of 1812 was notable for what?
options: It gave the United States control of Canadian land west of the Great Lakes
It required Britain to pay compensation to American shipowners
It created a Native American buffer state in the Old Northwest
It restored prewar boundaries and left the causes of the war unsettled
questions.explain: Both sides returned to the status quo ante bellum, and the issues that sparked the war had faded after Napoleon's defeat.

questions.q: The Hartford Convention of 1814-1815 was a meeting of which group?
options: Southern planters demanding secession from the Union
New England Federalists opposed to the war
questions.explain: Delegates aired grievances and proposed constitutional amendments, but news of victory at New Orleans left the Federalists looking unpatriotic.

questions.q: What was the long-term political result of the Hartford Convention?
questions.explain: Coming just before news of Jackson's victory and the peace, it made the Federalists appear disloyal and the party faded by the 1820s.

questions.q: The period after the War of 1812 with little partisan conflict is often called what?
questions.explain: With the Federalists in decline, James Monroe's presidency (1817-1825) saw one dominant party and a spirit of national unity.

questions.q: Which combination of policies made up Henry Clay's American System?
options: A high tariff only, with no national bank or road building by the federal government
A national bank and free trade, with road building left to the states
Direct taxes on farmers to pay for public schools and canals
A protective tariff, a national bank, and federally supported internal improvements
questions.explain: Clay wanted to link regional economies by protecting manufacturing, stabilizing currency, and funding roads and canals.

questions.q: The Second Bank of the United States was chartered in 1816 mainly to do what?
options: Provide cheap loans for settlers buying land in the Northwest
Collect state taxes for the federal government
Pay the pensions of Revolutionary War veterans directly
Provide a stable national currency and handle federal finances
questions.explain: After the War of 1812's financial troubles, Congress created a national bank to regulate currency and credit.

questions.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court struck down which state action?
options: Maryland's decision to charter a second state bank
Maryland's tax on the Second Bank of the United States
Maryland's ban on the import of foreign goods at Baltimore
Maryland's seizure of federal property near Baltimore
questions.explain: Marshall held that a state may not tax a federal institution, since 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy.'

questions.q: McCulloch v. Maryland expanded federal power by relying on which constitutional clause?
options: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
questions.explain: Marshall said the elastic clause allowed Congress to create a bank as a means of carrying out its enumerated powers.

questions.q: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) strengthened federal authority by ruling on what subject?
options: The authority of states to tax foreign ships
The power to regulate commerce between states
The question of whether new states could enter as slave states
The right of Congress to charter a national bank in any state
questions.explain: The Court held that Congress's power to regulate commerce included navigation between states, overriding a New York steamboat monopoly.

questions.q: Fletcher v. Peck (1810) was significant because the Court did what?
options: Upheld the first federal income tax
Struck down a state law for the first time
questions.explain: The ruling held that Georgia's repeal of a land grant violated the Constitution's Contract Clause.

questions.q: Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1819) protected what from state interference?
questions.explain: Marshall's Court ruled New Hampshire could not alter the college's charter, strengthening contract rights for private institutions and business.

questions.q: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and which other state as a free state?
questions.explain: Maine's admission kept the balance of free and slave states at twelve each in the Senate.

questions.q: The Missouri Compromise banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase territory north of what line?
options: The southern boundary of Pennsylvania, the Mason-Dixon Line
The northern edge of Louisiana at 49 degrees north
The course of the Ohio River from Pittsburgh to Cairo
questions.explain: Slavery was prohibited north of the line, except in Missouri itself.

questions.q: Which Kentucky leader was nicknamed the 'Great Compromiser' for helping pass the Missouri Compromise?
questions.explain: Clay, as Speaker of the House, worked to craft the compromise and later played the same role in 1833 and 1850.

questions.q: What did Thomas Jefferson mean when he said the Missouri crisis was like a 'fire bell in the night'?
options: It announced that Britain was preparing to attack New Orleans
It warned that slavery could tear the Union apart
It predicted a financial panic caused by western land sales
It marked the end of the Federalist Party's influence in Congress
questions.explain: Jefferson feared the geographic line between slave and free sections could eventually destroy the Union.

questions.q: The Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned which countries against intervening in the Western Hemisphere?
questions.explain: President Monroe declared the Americas closed to new colonization and said the United States would view European intervention as hostile.

questions.q: The principal author of the Monroe Doctrine was which Secretary of State?
questions.explain: Adams shaped the policy of American non-involvement in Europe and opposition to new European colonies in the Americas.

questions.q: In the Monroe Doctrine, the United States pledged to do what in European affairs?
options: Form a defensive alliance with Britain against Spain
Seek territory in South America to balance European empires
Guarantee the independence of Spain's colonies by sending American troops
Avoid interfering in European wars and in existing European colonies
questions.explain: Monroe pledged not to interfere with existing European colonies or wars while opposing new intervention in the Americas.

questions.q: The Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819 transferred which territory to the United States?
questions.explain: Spain ceded Florida and defined a western boundary of the Louisiana Purchase in exchange for the United States assuming certain claims.

questions.q: The presidential election of 1824 was decided in the House of Representatives. Who became president?
questions.explain: No candidate won an electoral majority; the House chose Adams, though Jackson had the most electoral and popular votes.

questions.q: Why did Jackson's supporters claim the 'corrupt bargain' in 1824-1825?
options: Jackson was denied electoral votes by a Senate ruling in Tennessee
Adams named Clay secretary of state after Clay backed him
Clay and Crawford agreed to split the western states between them
Henry Clay won the most electoral votes but gave the office to Adams
questions.explain: Jackson's allies saw Clay's appointment as a payoff, and the charge fueled Jackson's 1828 campaign.

questions.q: Which waterway, completed in 1825, linked the Great Lakes to the Atlantic through New York?
questions.explain: The Erie Canal connected Buffalo to Albany and the Hudson River, sharply cutting shipping costs.

questions.q: Which was a major economic effect of the Erie Canal?
options: It helped make New York City the nation's leading commercial city
It caused cotton plantations to spread to the Great Lakes region
It sharply reduced farm shipments from the Midwest to the East
It ended the use of steamboats on the Great Lakes
questions.explain: Western farm goods flowed east and manufactured goods moved west, boosting New York's rise.

questions.q: Robert Fulton's Clermont, launched in 1807, demonstrated the commercial value of what?
questions.explain: Steam power allowed boats to travel upstream and made river transport faster and more reliable.

questions.q: Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) made it easier to do what?
options: Weave cotton thread into finished cloth
Bale cotton for shipment down the Mississippi
Spin cotton into thread with water-powered machines
Remove seeds from short-staple cotton quickly
questions.explain: The cotton gin made short-staple cotton profitable, spreading cotton plantations across the Deep South.

questions.q: What was a major consequence of the cotton gin for slavery?
options: It made slavery less profitable and encouraged owners to free people
It moved most enslaved workers from the South to northern cities
It sharply increased the demand for enslaved labor in the Deep South
It persuaded planters that slavery had become too costly to keep
questions.explain: Cotton cultivation expanded rapidly, and the forced migration of enslaved people to the Deep South grew.

questions.q: Eli Whitney also promoted which manufacturing idea that influenced the 'American system of manufacturing'?
questions.explain: Interchangeable parts made weapons and other goods easier to produce and repair, a basis for later industry.

questions.q: The Lowell mills in Massachusetts hired young unmarried women from New England farms. They were often called what?
questions.explain: Mill owners provided boardinghouses and moral supervision to attract farm daughters to textile work.

questions.q: Which was a typical feature of the Lowell system of mill labor in the 1820s and 1830s?
options: Women lived in boardinghouses run by the owners
Workers were paid in land grants
Entire families worked together in company-owned barns
Children under ten ran the mills alone
questions.explain: Owners promised a respectable setting, though falling wages and longer hours later led to protests.

questions.q: The Waltham-Lowell system differed from earlier textile mills because it did what?
options: Relied on home production by farm families
Combined spinning and weaving in one factory
questions.explain: Francis Cabot Lowell's integrated factory brought all steps of cloth production under one roof.

questions.q: The Tariff of 1816 was passed to do what?
options: Raise money to pay for the construction of the Erie Canal
Reduce the prices of imported goods for western farmers
Pay off the national debt left over from the Revolution
Shield young manufacturers from cheap British imports
questions.explain: Cheap British goods flooded the market after the War of 1812, so Congress raised duties to protect domestic industry.

questions.q: The Cumberland (National) Road, begun in 1811, was important because it was what?
options: It was the first railroad connecting the Atlantic to the Mississippi
It was a military road built to invade Canada
It was the first major road built with federal money
It was the first railway tunnel built through the Appalachians
questions.explain: The road eventually ran west from Maryland toward the Ohio River, tying the Appalachian West to the East.

questions.q: Which novelist wrote 'The Last of the Mohicans' and helped found a distinctly American literature in the 1820s?
questions.explain: Cooper's frontier romances were among the first American novels widely read in Europe.

questions.q: The Hudson River School of painters is best known for what?
options: Formal portraits of presidents and generals
Realistic scenes of factory and city life
Large abstract paintings of frontier battles
questions.explain: Artists like Thomas Cole painted dramatic landscapes that expressed national pride in the American wilderness.

questions.q: The idea of Indian removal had roots before Jackson. Which president privately proposed in 1803 exchanging Native lands east of the Mississippi for lands in the West?
questions.explain: Jefferson privately suggested exchanging lands east of the Mississippi for lands in Louisiana, an early version of removal thinking.

questions.q: The Seminole resisted American control in Florida in conflicts that began with Andrew Jackson's 1818 invasion. That conflict is known as what?
questions.explain: Jackson's incursion into Spanish Florida helped convince Spain to cede the territory.

questions.q: The Rush-Bagot Agreement (1817) limited naval forces on which waters?
questions.explain: The United States and Britain agreed to demilitarize the Great Lakes, an early step in peaceful border relations.

questions.q: The Convention of 1818 set the US-British Canadian boundary west to the Rocky Mountains along which line?
questions.explain: The treaty also provided for joint occupation of the Oregon Country for ten years.

questions.q: The American Colonization Society, founded in 1816, aimed to do what?
options: Pay slaveholders to free the people they held in the South
Organize armed uprisings to end slavery in Virginia
Return free Black Americans to the states where they were born
Resettle free Black Americans in Africa
questions.explain: The society's work led to the founding of Liberia, but many Black Americans and abolitionists opposed colonization.

questions.q: Chief Justice John Marshall served as a leader of which party before joining the Court?
questions.explain: Marshall was a Federalist who shaped constitutional law for 34 years and increased the Court's power.

questions.q: Which Federalist Supreme Court justice did Jefferson's Republican allies impeach in 1804, only to see the Senate acquit him in 1805?
questions.explain: The House impeached Justice Chase but the Senate failed to convict him, preserving judicial independence.

questions.q: Aaron Burr killed which political rival in a duel in 1804?
questions.explain: Burr, the sitting vice president, shot Hamilton at Weehawken, New Jersey, and Hamilton died the next day.

questions.q: The 1807 treason trial of Aaron Burr ended with what result?
questions.explain: Chief Justice Marshall's strict definition of treason led to Burr's acquittal on charges of plotting a western conspiracy.

questions.q: The Land Act of 1820 made it easier for ordinary settlers to buy western land by doing what?
options: Giving public land free to Revolutionary War veterans
Lowering the price per acre and the minimum purchase
Requiring buyers to farm the land for five years before payment
Tax western settlers to pay for canals in the East
questions.explain: Congress cut the price to $1.25 an acre and allowed purchases of 80 acres, though cash payment was required.

questions.q: The Panic of 1819 was a major financial crisis and depression in the young republic. What contributed to it?
options: A British naval blockade of American ports
Land speculation and tightened credit by the Second Bank
The sudden loss of the Louisiana Territory to Spain
A federal ban on state-chartered banks across the country
questions.explain: Overextended banks and falling crop prices led to foreclosures, unemployment, and distrust of banks.

questions.q: How did Jefferson's Republican Congress respond to the Federalist Judiciary Act of 1801?
options: It doubled the number of Supreme Court justices
It required all federal judges to stand for election
It repealed the law creating new federal judgeships
It ordered the removal of Chief Justice John Marshall
questions.explain: Republicans repealed the 1801 law that had created new judgeships filled by Adams's midnight appointees.

questions.q: Which architect, hired by Jefferson in 1803, redesigned the Capitol's wings and directed their rebuilding after the British burned them in 1814?
questions.explain: Benjamin Henry Latrobe served as Surveyor of Public Buildings under Jefferson and Madison and rebuilt the burned Capitol wings; Charles Bulfinch later completed the building.

questions.q: After the British burned the Executive Mansion in 1814, which architect oversaw its reconstruction?
questions.explain: Hoban, the original architect, rebuilt the mansion, which was ready for Monroe in 1817.

questions.q: Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary reflected which cultural aim?
options: To copy British spelling and pronunciation exactly
To record the vocabulary of Native American languages
To create a distinctly American English
To standardize Latin and Greek teaching in American colleges
questions.explain: Webster promoted American spellings and usage as part of building a distinct national culture.

questions.q: John Deere's steel plow, introduced in 1837, helped farmers by letting them do what?
options: Pick cotton more rapidly on large Southern plantations
Cut the canals that linked the Great Lakes to the East
Mine coal in the Appalachian foothills for new steam engines
Break the tough sod of the prairies and farm the Midwest
questions.explain: John Deere's self-scouring plow made Midwestern farming far more productive.

questions.q: Cyrus McCormick's mechanical reaper (patented 1834) did what for agriculture?
options: Plant seeds in straight rows across large fields
Separate cotton fiber from its seeds in the field
Sort and weigh cotton at river ports before shipment
Speed up the harvesting of wheat and other grain crops
questions.explain: The reaper allowed one farmer to harvest far more wheat and encouraged large-scale commercial farming.

questions.q: Andrew Jackson won the presidency in 1828 and drew strong support from which group?
options: Wealthy merchants and bankers of New England
Farmers, urban workers, and frontier settlers
Wealthy Boston and New York bankers and manufacturers
questions.explain: Jackson presented himself as a champion of the common man against eastern elites, and the electorate had grown as states dropped property requirements.

questions.q: Which change made the 1828 election different from earlier ones?
options: Women gained the vote in several western states
More white men could vote after property rules ended
Voters in every state chose presidential electors directly
Property requirements were added in most western states
questions.explain: Between 1810 and 1830 many states removed property qualifications, expanding the electorate of white men.

questions.q: Critics who disliked Jackson's use of the veto and presidential power nicknamed him what?
questions.explain: Opponents said Jackson acted like a monarch, and the Whig Party took its name from the British party that opposed royal power.

questions.q: The 'spoils system' associated with Jackson refers to what practice?
options: Dividing the Treasury's surplus among states
questions.explain: Jackson defended rotation in office as democratic, though it let party loyalty influence federal appointments.

questions.q: Jackson relied on an informal circle of unofficial advisers whom critics nicknamed what?
questions.explain: Jackson often relied on close friends and editors rather than his formal cabinet.

questions.q: The Petticoat Affair divided Jackson's cabinet over the treatment of which person?
options: Dolley Madison, whose parties were criticized by the cabinet
Peggy Eaton, wife of the secretary of war
Floride Calhoun, whose husband resigned as vice president
Louisa Adams, the wife of the president
questions.explain: Washington society shunned Peggy Eaton, and the controversy helped push the cabinet's resignation and Calhoun's break with Jackson.

questions.q: The Tariff of 1828, which southerners called the Tariff of Abominations, was opposed mainly because it did what?
options: Placed heavy taxes on cotton sold to Britain
Created a national bank with branches across the South
Lowered duties on British cloth and iron
Raised the cost of imported goods the South depended on
questions.explain: The high duties protected northern manufacturers while raising the cost of goods for the cotton South.

questions.q: Which South Carolinian wrote the theory of nullification in his anonymous South Carolina Exposition and Protest?
questions.explain: Calhoun argued that a state could declare a federal law void within its borders, a doctrine echoing Jefferson and Madison's 1798 resolutions.

questions.q: In the 1830 Webster-Hayne debate in the Senate, Daniel Webster defended what idea?
options: That states had the right to leave the Union at will
That the Union was perpetual, not just a compact of states
That western land should be sold only to settlers from the South
That nullification was a legitimate remedy for any state
questions.explain: Webster ended with the line 'Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable.'

questions.q: At the 1830 Jefferson Day dinner, Jackson offered a toast aimed at nullifiers. What did it say in substance?
options: 'Our Federal Union: it must be preserved'
'The Constitution is a compact of sovereigns'
questions.explain: Jackson's toast signaled he would oppose nullification; Calhoun answered with a toast ranking liberty above the Union.

questions.q: South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification declared what?
options: South Carolina had left the Union and formed a new country
The Second Bank of the United States was illegal in the state
The tariffs of 1828 and 1832 were void in the state
That slaveholding was protected by the state constitution
questions.explain: The convention declared the tariffs unenforceable in South Carolina after February 1833.

questions.q: How did Jackson respond to the Nullification Crisis?
options: He sought the Force Bill to enforce the tariff
He signed a law allowing South Carolina to ignore the tariff
He refused to act and let the state's law stand
He offered to remove federal troops from Charleston
questions.explain: Jackson issued a proclamation against nullification and obtained the Force Bill, while also backing tariff reduction.

questions.q: What ended the Nullification Crisis in 1833?
options: A Supreme Court ruling for South Carolina
A compromise tariff that slowly lowered duties
questions.explain: Henry Clay's Compromise Tariff reduced rates over a decade, and South Carolina rescinded its ordinance, though it nullified the Force Bill.

questions.q: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 authorized the president to do what?
options: Trade lands east of the Mississippi for lands in the West
Give citizenship to Native Americans who left their homelands
Create independent Native states within existing state borders
Divide Native lands equally among the existing states
questions.explain: The law led to the forced relocation of southeastern nations to Indian Territory.

questions.q: Which five southeastern Native nations were the main targets of Jackson's removal policy?
options: Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, and Apache
Iroquois, Mohawk, Seneca, Oneida, and Cayuga
Navajo, Hopi, Zuni, Pueblo, and Ute
Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole
questions.explain: These southeastern nations held fertile homelands that settlers and states wanted, and most were forced to move to Indian Territory.

questions.q: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Supreme Court ruled that what?
options: The Cherokee had to move west
States could extend laws over reservations
Georgia had no authority over Cherokee lands
questions.explain: Marshall held that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct political community in which Georgia's laws had no force.

questions.q: Jackson is traditionally said to have responded to Worcester v. Georgia by suggesting what?
options: That the Court could not enforce its ruling
That he would appoint a new chief justice
questions.explain: Whether he spoke the famous words is uncertain, but he did not act to enforce the ruling, and Georgia continued its policies.

questions.q: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) described the Cherokee as what?
questions.explain: Marshall refused to hear the case as an original suit but used this term to describe the tribe's relationship to the United States.

questions.q: The 1835 Treaty of New Echota, which led to Cherokee removal, was controversial because it was signed by whom?
options: Principal Chief John Ross and the elected council
Delegates elected by every Cherokee town
A small faction without the nation's authority
Congress alone, without any Cherokee participation
questions.explain: Most Cherokee, led by John Ross, rejected the treaty, but it was ratified and enforced anyway.

questions.q: The forced march of the Cherokee to Indian Territory in 1838-1839 is known as what?
questions.explain: Thousands of Cherokee died of exposure, disease, and hunger on the journey west.

questions.q: Which Cherokee leader led the nation's legal and political resistance to removal?
questions.explain: Ross served as principal chief and pursued petitions and lawsuits to protect Cherokee land.

questions.q: Which Cherokee man created a writing system for his people in the 1820s?
questions.explain: Sequoyah's syllabary allowed rapid literacy, and the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper began in 1828.

questions.q: Which Native nation fought the Second Seminole War (1835-1842) to avoid removal from Florida?
questions.explain: Led by figures such as Osceola, Seminole resisters made it among the costliest Indian wars for the United States.

questions.q: The Black Hawk War of 1832 was fought largely over lands in which region?
questions.explain: Sauk and Fox people led by Black Hawk tried to return to lands in Illinois and were defeated.

questions.q: In Jackson's 'Bank War,' he opposed the Second Bank of the United States because he believed it did what?
options: It concentrated power in a wealthy unaccountable elite
Printed so little currency that farmers could not borrow
Was controlled entirely by the state governments
Refused to hold any federal deposits in its vaults
questions.explain: Jackson viewed the bank as a monopoly favoring eastern financiers and, in his view, a threat to liberty.

questions.q: In 1832 Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States. Who led the bank at the time?
questions.explain: Biddle, the bank's president, tried to push early recharter in an election year and Jackson used the veto against it.

questions.q: After winning reelection in 1832, Jackson weakened the Bank by moving federal deposits into what?
questions.explain: Jackson ordered Treasury funds placed in selected state banks, which critics derided as pet banks.

questions.q: In 1834 the Senate voted to do what to President Jackson over his removal of Bank deposits?
questions.explain: The Senate passed a censure resolution; Jackson's allies later had it expunged from the record.

questions.q: The Specie Circular of 1836 required what?
options: Paper money from the Second Bank for all land purchases
A halt to all sales of federal land in the West
Gold or silver coin for purchases of public land
Silver bars delivered to the Treasury in Washington
questions.explain: Jackson issued the order to curb land speculation fueled by paper money, which drained gold from eastern banks.

questions.q: The Panic of 1837 was followed by a long depression. Which factor helped cause it?
options: A British invasion of the Great Lakes region
The loss of the Erie Canal's shipping revenue
A sudden end to cotton exports caused by war with Britain
Land speculation, bank failures, and tight credit
questions.explain: Overextended credit and falling cotton prices combined with tight specie to trigger bank failures and unemployment.

questions.q: Martin Van Buren's response to the Panic of 1837 was to propose what?
options: An Independent Treasury apart from private banks
A third national bank to restore confidence in paper money
A public works program to employ jobless workers
Higher tariffs on all European imports
questions.explain: Van Buren favored limited government action and eventually obtained the Independent Treasury in 1840.

questions.q: The Whig Party formed in the 1830s mainly in opposition to whom?
questions.explain: Whigs, led by figures like Clay and Webster, favored congressional leadership and economic development against 'executive tyranny.'

questions.q: Which policy did Whigs generally support?
options: Free trade, state banks, and strict limits on federal spending
A national bank, protective tariffs, and internal improvements
Abolition of the tariff and an end to western land sales
A strict ban on federal spending for roads and canals
questions.explain: Whigs backed a national bank, protective tariffs and federally funded roads and canals, a program based on Henry Clay's American System.

questions.q: The 1840 presidential campaign of William Henry Harrison used which popular slogan and image?
options: 'Fifty-four forty or fight' and the Oregon boundary
'Remember the Alamo' and the cause of Texas
'Tippecanoe and Tyler Too' and the log cabin image
'Manifest Destiny' and the settlement of Texas
questions.explain: Whigs portrayed the wealthy Harrison as a common man in a log cabin and used mass rallies and songs.

questions.q: After William Henry Harrison died in 1841 only a month into his term, who became president?
questions.explain: Tyler was the first vice president to take the presidency on a president's death, setting a precedent for succession.

questions.q: John Tyler vetoed Whig bank bills and nearly his whole cabinet resigned in protest. Which member stayed on?
questions.explain: Webster remained long enough to complete the Webster-Ashburton negotiations with Britain.

questions.q: The Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 settled a boundary dispute between the United States and Britain in which region?
options: The boundary of the Oregon Country at the Pacific coast
The southern boundary of Texas along the Rio Grande
The Maine and New Brunswick border
The border between Georgia and Florida
questions.explain: The treaty settled the Maine-New Brunswick border after the Aroostook confrontation.

questions.q: The Second Great Awakening was a wave of what?
options: A spread of scientific societies in American cities
A rapid growth of political parties after 1800
A wave of religious revivals in the early 1800s
A movement against organized religion and public schools
questions.explain: Preachers held camp meetings and revivals that stressed personal salvation and moral reform.

questions.q: Which preacher led massive revivals in upstate New York in the 1820s and 1830s and urged converts toward reform?
questions.explain: Finney's 'new measures' emphasized free will and moral activism, inspiring reform movements.

questions.q: The Second Great Awakening encouraged reform movements by teaching what?
options: That individuals and society could be improved
That religion should separate from daily life
questions.explain: Revivalists said people could choose salvation and should work to perfect society, feeding temperance, abolition, and other causes.

questions.q: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints was founded in the 1830s by whom?
questions.explain: Smith organized the church in New York in 1830, and followers later migrated west seeking refuge.

questions.q: The Mormon migration to Utah in 1846-1847 was led by which leader?
questions.explain: After Smith was killed in Illinois in 1844, Young led the Latter-day Saints to the Great Salt Lake valley.

questions.q: The temperance movement of the early 1800s urged people to do what?
options: Gain the vote for women nationwide
questions.explain: Reformers saw drinking as a cause of poverty and family violence, and by the 1850s some states banned it.

questions.q: The Maine Law of 1851 was significant because it did what?
options: Created public high schools in every Maine town
Limited the work day in Maine's mills to ten hours
Banned the sale of alcohol across the state of Maine
questions.explain: Maine's law became a model for other states' prohibition measures.

questions.q: Which reformer led the push for better treatment of the mentally ill in prisons and asylums?
questions.explain: Dix lobbied states and Congress to build and improve state hospitals for the mentally ill.

questions.q: Horace Mann is best known for promoting what cause?
questions.explain: As Massachusetts education secretary, Mann pushed for tax-supported schools and trained teachers.

questions.q: Thomas Gallaudet is known for his work in educating which group?
questions.explain: Gallaudet helped found the first permanent school for the deaf in the United States, in Hartford in 1817.

questions.q: William Lloyd Garrison's newspaper The Liberator demanded what?
questions.explain: Garrison began the paper in 1831 and called for immediate emancipation without compensation to slaveholders.

questions.q: Which approach did the American Anti-Slavery Society, founded in 1833, mainly rely on at first?
options: Armed uprisings aimed at freeing enslaved people in the South
Gradual compensation to slaveholders for their losses
Campaigns to build a new national party and nothing else
Moral appeals and pamphlets urging immediate emancipation
questions.explain: Garrisonians used pamphlets, speeches, and petitions, though members later disagreed over politics and tactics.

questions.q: Which sisters from South Carolina became prominent abolitionists and women's rights advocates?
questions.explain: The Grimke sisters, from a slaveholding family, spoke publicly against slavery in the 1830s.

questions.q: Sojourner Truth is known as what?
options: The organizer of the Seneca Falls convention of 1848
A formerly enslaved speaker for abolition and women's rights
The publisher of the abolitionist newspaper The Liberator
The author of the novel Uncle Tom's Cabin
questions.explain: Born into slavery in New York, Truth became a powerful speaker for abolition and women's rights.

questions.q: The congressional 'gag rule' of 1836-1844 did what?
options: Banned the mailing of abolitionist newspapers in the South
Tabled antislavery petitions in the House automatically
Limited all Senate speeches on slavery to ten minutes
Required all petitions to Congress to come from landowners
questions.explain: The rule blocked discussion of petitions against slavery until John Quincy Adams helped win its repeal.

questions.q: Which former president fought the gag rule as a member of the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: Adams, called 'Old Man Eloquent,' defended the right to petition and finally saw the rule repealed in 1844.

questions.q: Elijah Lovejoy, an abolitionist editor, was killed in 1837 by what?
options: A federal marshal enforcing a court order in Missouri
A duel with a rival editor in St. Louis
An accident at his printing press in Boston
A proslavery mob in Alton, Illinois
questions.explain: His death made him a martyr for the antislavery cause and for press freedom.

questions.q: Harriet Tubman is best known for doing what?
options: Writing a bestselling novel about plantation life
Editing an abolitionist newspaper in Rochester
Leading enslaved people north to freedom
Founding the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833
questions.explain: Tubman escaped slavery in 1849 and made many return trips to guide others north.

questions.q: The Underground Railroad was best described as what?
options: A steam railroad line built by abolitionists to carry fugitives
A network of people and safe places aiding escapes
A federal program that bought freedom for enslaved people
A colony in Canada created for free Black Americans
questions.explain: It was a loose network of conductors, stations, and routes rather than an actual railroad.

questions.q: Which formerly enslaved man published a bestselling 1845 autobiography after escaping from Maryland?
questions.explain: Douglass's autobiography became a bestseller and made him an international voice against slavery.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 by doing what?
options: Crossing the Ohio River by raft
Hiding on a ship to England
Following a Quaker guide to Canada
Traveling north disguised as a sailor
questions.explain: Douglass used papers borrowed from a free Black sailor and reached New York.

questions.q: The newspaper Douglass founded in Rochester, New York, in 1847 was called what?
questions.explain: Douglass launched the paper to give a Black voice to antislavery and later joined political abolitionism.

questions.q: Freedom's Journal, begun in 1827, was notable as what?
options: The first national antislavery society's journal
A Quaker pamphlet attacking the slave trade
The first Black-owned newspaper in the country
A newspaper published by the federal government
questions.explain: Samuel Cornish and John Russwurm published it in New York City.

questions.q: David Walker's 1829 'Appeal to the Colored Citizens of the World' was notable because it did what?
options: It defended gradual emancipation and colonization
It called for the creation of a separate Black state in Canada
It urged enslaved people to resist and condemned slavery and racism
It argued for compensating slaveholders who freed enslaved people
questions.explain: Walker's pamphlet circulated widely in the South and alarmed slaveholders.

questions.q: Nat Turner's 1831 rebellion took place in which state?
questions.explain: Turner led enslaved people in Southampton County, killing about 55 white people before the revolt was crushed.

questions.q: After Nat Turner's rebellion, many southern states did what?
options: Tightened laws on enslaved and free Black people
Began plans for gradual emancipation in Virginia
Offered land grants to freed families in the Upper South
Banned the sale of Southern cotton to northern mills
questions.explain: States restricted assembly, education, and travel, and slaveholders defended slavery more aggressively.

questions.q: The Amistad case of 1839-1841 involved what?
options: A shipwreck that killed several American whalers off Cape Cod
A British blockade of southern ports during a trade dispute
Africans who seized a slave ship and won freedom in court
A mutiny aboard a US Navy ship off Florida
questions.explain: The Supreme Court ruled that the captives had been illegally enslaved, with John Quincy Adams arguing their case.

questions.q: The Creole incident of 1841 involved which event?
options: Enslaved people seized a ship and sailed to the Bahamas
Sailors on a US navy ship staged a mutiny off the coast of Florida
A British ship captured a slave vessel and sold its cargo in Cuba
A British seizure of an American ship in the Caribbean
questions.explain: The case caused diplomatic tension between the United States and Britain over slavery and ships' cargo.

questions.q: By the 1850s, which crop dominated the economy and exports of the antebellum South?
questions.explain: Cotton accounted for more than half of US exports and drove the demand for enslaved labor.

questions.q: Which practice split many enslaved families in the antebellum South?
options: The domestic slave trade from the Upper South to the Deep South
A federal program that moved enslaved families to western territories
The practice of renting enslaved workers to northern factories
The colonization of enslaved families in Liberia
questions.explain: Hundreds of thousands of enslaved people were sold and moved south and west as cotton spread.

questions.q: Which of the following was true of most white southerners before the Civil War?
options: They did not own enslaved people
They owned more than ten enslaved people
questions.explain: Fewer than a third of southern white families held slaves, though slaveholders dominated wealth and politics.

questions.q: Which immigrant group arrived in large numbers in the 1840s fleeing a potato famine?
questions.explain: A famine that began in 1845 drove huge Irish migration, mostly to northeastern cities.

questions.q: Large numbers of German immigrants in the 1840s and 1850s mostly settled where?
options: The Deep South, where they bought cotton plantations
The Midwest, especially Wisconsin and Ohio
The New England mill towns of Massachusetts
questions.explain: Many Germans became farmers and city residents in the Midwest and kept their language and customs.

questions.q: Nativist groups of the 1840s and 1850s opposed what?
options: Westward expansion into the Oregon Country
Public education supported by state taxes
The temperance movement and efforts to ban alcohol
questions.explain: Many nativists feared that Irish and German Catholics threatened Protestant and republican values.

questions.q: The American Party, whose members were nicknamed the 'Know-Nothings,' arose in the 1850s because of what?
options: Opposition to the Mexican War and its costs
Support for the immediate abolition of slavery
questions.explain: Members were told to say 'I know nothing' about the secret order, and the party won many local and state offices in 1854.

questions.q: Which essayist argued in 'Self-Reliance' that individuals should trust their own conscience over conformity?
questions.explain: Emerson was the leading voice of Transcendentalism, which stressed intuition and individualism.

questions.q: Henry David Thoreau's essay 'Resistance to Civil Government' (Civil Disobedience) argued for what?
options: Refusing to obey unjust laws and accepting the penalty
Overthrowing the government by force when laws are unjust
Withdrawing from political life to live in isolation
Paying taxes to support a strong national bank
questions.explain: Thoreau went to jail in 1846 rather than pay a tax tied to slavery and the Mexican War, and his essay later influenced Gandhi and King.

questions.q: The poem collection 'Leaves of Grass' was written by which poet?
questions.explain: Whitman celebrated democracy and the common person in free verse, first publishing the book in 1855.

questions.q: Nathaniel Hawthorne's 'The Scarlet Letter' and Herman Melville's 'Moby-Dick' are examples of what?
questions.explain: The 1850s saw a burst of distinctive American literature that explored sin, conscience, and the national character.

questions.q: Utopian communities such as Brook Farm and New Harmony were created to do what?
options: Escape from military service during the War of 1812
Support slaveholding planters in the new western territories
Experiment with new ways of living and sharing property
Convert Native peoples to Christianity on the frontier
questions.explain: These communities experimented with shared property or cooperative labor, and most lasted only a few years.

questions.q: The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 launched what movement?
options: The antislavery movement in New York
The movement for free public schools
questions.explain: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized the convention in upstate New York.

questions.q: The Declaration of Sentiments at Seneca Falls was modeled on which document?
options: The Constitution's preamble and Bill of Rights
The Mayflower Compact and colonial charters
questions.explain: It declared that 'all men and women are created equal' and listed grievances about women's legal status.

questions.q: Which resolution at Seneca Falls was the most controversial, passing narrowly with Douglass's support?
options: Requiring women to serve on juries
Calling for women's right to vote
questions.explain: Stanton's suffrage resolution seemed radical even to some attendees, but Frederick Douglass spoke in its favor.

questions.q: Which woman, with Susan B. Anthony, later co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association in 1869?
questions.explain: Stanton and Anthony formed the NWSA after the movement split over the Fifteenth Amendment.

questions.q: Which notable change in women's status did the 1848 New York Married Women's Property Act begin to produce?
options: Allowed married women to own property in their own names
Gave married women the right to vote in state elections
Let women serve on juries in New York courts
Required public schools for girls in every county
questions.explain: The state laws of the 1840s began to relax coverture, giving women more control over property.

questions.q: The 'cult of domesticity' in the early 1800s taught what idea?
options: That a woman's proper place was the home
That women should enter factories to support national growth
That women should seek political office in state governments
That women should vote and hold public office
questions.explain: This ideal shaped middle-class expectations while many women worked for wages or on farms and plantations.

questions.q: The Oneida Community and Shaker villages are examples of what?
options: Plantations that used enslaved labor to grow cotton
Labor unions formed by textile mill workers
Native American reservations in the Midwest
questions.explain: Such groups tried to build perfect societies on religious principles.

questions.q: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent was called what?
questions.explain: The phrase, popularized in 1845, expressed the idea that American expansion was both inevitable and justified.

questions.q: Which journalist is traditionally credited with coining the term 'Manifest Destiny' in 1845?
questions.explain: O'Sullivan used the phrase while writing about the annexation of Texas.

questions.q: Texas won independence from Mexico in 1836 after what battle?
questions.explain: Sam Houston's army defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto, leading to the Republic of Texas.

questions.q: Slavery was a central issue in the Texas question because Mexico had done what?
options: Abolished slavery, while many American settlers in Texas held enslaved people
Required all settlers to convert to Catholicism while Texans wanted Protestantism
Sold Texas to the United States, which then banned slavery there
Banned all American settlement, which the settlers openly welcomed
questions.explain: Mexico outlawed slavery in 1829 and tried to limit American migration, which fed settler resistance.

questions.q: Why did Presidents Jackson and Van Buren hesitate to annex the Republic of Texas?
options: They believed Texas had asked to remain independent permanently
They thought Congress had already banned all western expansion
They expected the Supreme Court to bar annexation by treaty
Annexation would inflame the slavery dispute and risk war
questions.explain: Annexation would add a large slave state and likely trigger conflict with Mexico, so northern opposition mattered.

questions.q: Texas was annexed in 1845 by what method?
options: A treaty approved by two-thirds of the Senate
questions.explain: After the Senate rejected an 1844 annexation treaty, supporters used a joint resolution that needed only majorities.

questions.q: James K. Polk won the 1844 election on a platform that favored what?
questions.explain: Polk, a Democrat and expansionist, defeated Henry Clay, who hedged on Texas.

questions.q: The Democratic campaign slogan 'Fifty-four forty or fight' referred to claims in which region?
questions.explain: Expansionists demanded all of Oregon up to latitude 54 degrees 40 minutes north.

questions.q: The Oregon Treaty of 1846 with Britain did what?
options: Gave all of the Oregon Country to the United States
Gave all of Oregon to Britain
Divided the Oregon Country at the 49th parallel
questions.explain: The Oregon Treaty of 1846 split the Oregon Country with Britain at the 49th parallel. Polk compromised rather than risk war with Britain while tensions with Mexico grew.

questions.q: Families who traveled west in wagon trains in the 1840s mostly followed which route to Oregon?
questions.explain: Tens of thousands of settlers crossed the plains and mountains on this route starting in the 1840s.

questions.q: The Mexican-American War began in 1846 after a clash over a disputed zone along which boundary?
options: The land between the Sabine River and the Red River
The strip along the Gila River in present-day Arizona
The land between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande
The valley of the Colorado River near the Pacific
questions.explain: Polk sent troops into the disputed area, and a skirmish there led him to say American blood had been shed on American soil.

questions.q: Which representative challenged Polk's claim that Mexico started the war by demanding to know the 'spot' where blood was shed?
questions.explain: Freshman Congressman Lincoln's 'Spot Resolutions' questioned whether the fighting occurred on American soil.

questions.q: The Mexican-American War ended in 1848 with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. What did Mexico give up?
options: California and much of the present-day Southwest
Only the state of Texas, up to the Nueces River
Florida and the Gulf Coast west to Louisiana
A strip of southern Arizona for a railroad route
questions.explain: Mexico ceded roughly half its territory, including California and New Mexico, and the US paid 15 million dollars.

questions.q: What did the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo promise to Mexicans living in the ceded territory?
options: They had to leave the territory within one year
They would be moved onto reservations in the new territory
They could become US citizens and keep their property
They would remain Mexican citizens under US law
questions.explain: The treaty promised property rights and the choice of citizenship, though these promises were often poorly kept.

questions.q: The Mexican-American War's major battles in Mexico included the capture of which capital by General Winfield Scott in 1847?
questions.explain: Scott's army landed at Veracruz and marched inland to take Mexico City, ending organized resistance.

questions.q: Which pair of future Civil War generals both served as officers in the Mexican-American War?
options: Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee
Nathan Bedford Forrest and John Bell Hood
Oliver O. Howard and Joshua Chamberlain
questions.explain: Grant and Lee both served in Mexico, as did many other later commanders, including McClellan, Meade, and Stonewall Jackson.

questions.q: The Wilmot Proviso (1846) proposed what?
options: Admission of California as a slave state
A ban on slavery in land taken from Mexico
An immediate end to the Mexican-American War
A plan to buy Cuba from Spain for the South
questions.explain: David Wilmot's amendment passed the House repeatedly but failed in the Senate, deepening the sectional divide.

questions.q: Which doctrine let settlers in a territory decide for themselves whether to allow slavery?
questions.explain: Lewis Cass and others proposed letting territorial voters decide the slavery question.

questions.q: The Free-Soil Party of 1848 opposed what?
options: Restricting immigration from Ireland and Germany
Ending the Mexican War before any land was taken
The spread of slavery into the western territories
Raising the tariff to protect northern industry
questions.explain: Free-Soilers ran Martin Van Buren and argued that slavery should be barred from new lands to protect free labor.

questions.q: General Zachary Taylor won the presidency in 1848 as a candidate of which party?
questions.explain: The Whigs chose the war hero Taylor, who had no clear political record.

questions.q: The discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill in 1848 led to what?
questions.explain: Tens of thousands of migrants rushed to California in 1849, known as the forty-niners.

questions.q: The California Gold Rush led to rapid statehood for California because it did what?
options: The Compromise of 1850 forced California to join at once
Mexican officials requested admission to the Union
Congress needed the state to balance Texas
A flood of migrants quickly created a large population
questions.explain: California's population surged and it applied for statehood as a free state in 1849-1850.

questions.q: Which agreement admitted California as a free state and enacted a stricter fugitive slave law?
questions.explain: A package of laws in September 1850 admitted California and addressed other territorial and slavery issues.

questions.q: Which Kentucky senator introduced the compromise package that became the Compromise of 1850?
questions.explain: Clay's proposals were then reshaped and passed by Stephen Douglas as separate bills.

questions.q: Stephen Douglas helped pass the Compromise of 1850 by doing what?
options: He used a filibuster to wear down the opposition
He gained a presidential veto override on the Fugitive Slave Act
He secured a Supreme Court ruling approving the compromise
He split the omnibus bill into separate measures
questions.explain: After the omnibus bill failed, Douglas guided individual measures through Congress.

questions.q: In his March 1850 speech supporting compromise, Daniel Webster angered many northerners by backing which measure?
options: Admitting Texas as a free state
questions.explain: Webster's Seventh of March speech defended compromise and drew attacks from antislavery New Englanders.

questions.q: Which senator, dying in 1850, argued that the South could only be protected if the North stopped agitating the slavery question?
questions.explain: Calhoun's final Senate argument was read for him because he was too ill to speak.

questions.q: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required what?
options: Northern states to pay for the freedom of fugitives
Border states to free their enslaved people gradually
Southern states to end the interstate slave trade
Citizens to aid in catching runaways, with no jury trial
questions.explain: The law made federal commissioners decide cases and penalized officials who failed to return alleged runaways.

questions.q: What was a common northern response to the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850?
options: A sudden rise in northern support for slaveholders
The end of the Underground Railroad's activity
A mass migration of Black northerners to the South
questions.explain: The act drew thousands of northerners into resisting enforcement, and some states passed personal liberty laws.

questions.q: Which 1852 novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe showed northern readers the human cost of slavery?
options: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
questions.explain: The bestselling novel intensified antislavery sentiment in the North and angered the South.

questions.q: Which law banned the slave trade in the District of Columbia while leaving slavery itself legal there?
questions.explain: The Compromise banned the sale of enslaved people in the capital while leaving slavery itself legal there.

questions.q: The Compromise of 1850 settled the status of the Utah and New Mexico territories by applying what principle?
questions.explain: Voters in the territories would decide whether to allow slavery when they sought statehood.

questions.q: Commodore Matthew Perry's 1853-1854 expedition aimed to do what?
questions.explain: Perry used a show of naval force to secure the Treaty of Kanagawa, opening Japanese ports to US ships.

questions.q: The Gadsden Purchase of 1853 bought land from Mexico for what purpose?
options: A naval base on the Pacific coast
New plantation land for slaveholders in Texas
Control of a possible canal across Central Mexico
A southern route for a transcontinental railroad
questions.explain: The strip of land in southern Arizona and New Mexico suited a southern railroad route.

questions.q: Stephen Douglas's Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 did what?
options: Banned slavery in both new territories permanently
Admitted Kansas to the Union as a free state at once
Admitted Nebraska to the Union as a slave state
Created two territories and applied popular sovereignty
questions.explain: Douglas's bill applied popular sovereignty to lands the Missouri Compromise had closed to slavery.

questions.q: The Kansas-Nebraska Act effectively repealed what earlier agreement?
options: The Compromise of 1850 and its fugitive slave law
The Northwest Ordinance's ban on slavery above the Ohio
questions.explain: Opening northern territory to slavery by local choice angered many northerners.

questions.q: Which political party formed in 1854 in response to the Kansas-Nebraska Act?
questions.explain: Antislavery Whigs, Free-Soilers, and northern Democrats united in the new party opposing the expansion of slavery.

questions.q: The Republican Party's main position in the 1850s on slavery was what?
options: To end slavery everywhere in the country immediately
To defend slavery in the Southern states
To let each territory vote on slavery by popular sovereignty
To stop slavery from spreading into the territories
questions.explain: Republicans mostly pledged not to touch slavery where it existed but to bar its spread.

questions.q: The term 'Bleeding Kansas' refers to what?
options: A deadly flood that struck Kansas towns
A war between settlers and Native nations
Violence between proslavery and antislavery settlers
A disease that killed cattle on the plains
questions.explain: Rival governments and armed groups fought over whether Kansas would be slave or free.

questions.q: Proslavery Missourians who crossed into Kansas to vote in 1855 were known as what?
questions.explain: Thousands crossed the border to influence territorial elections, helping create a proslavery legislature.

questions.q: In 1856 John Brown led the killing of five proslavery settlers at which place in Kansas?
questions.explain: Brown's attack on the night of May 24-25 was a response to the sack of Lawrence and the caning of Sumner.

questions.q: In May 1856, Senator Charles Sumner was beaten with a cane on the Senate floor by whom?
questions.explain: Brooks, a South Carolina congressman, attacked Sumner after Sumner's speech 'The Crime Against Kansas' insulted Brooks's relative.

questions.q: Preston Brooks attacked Sumner in response to what?
options: Sumner's vote against a southern tariff bill
A duel challenge Sumner had issued to Brooks
Sumner's attack on proslavery forces and Senator Butler
An article Sumner had published about Brooks's family
questions.explain: Sumner's 'Crime Against Kansas' speech ridiculed Butler, Brooks's elderly cousin.

questions.q: What was the consequence for Preston Brooks after the caning of Sumner?
options: He was expelled from Congress by a two-thirds vote
He was fined and resigned, then was reelected
He was sent to prison for assault
He lost his seat and left politics for good
questions.explain: The House failed to expel him; he resigned, then won a special election and was hailed by many southerners.

questions.q: The Old Senate Chamber, where the Sumner caning occurred, was used by which body from 1860 until 1935?
questions.explain: After the Senate moved to its new chamber in 1859, the Supreme Court took over the old room, where it met until its own building opened.

questions.q: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), the Supreme Court ruled that what?
options: Dred Scott was free because he had lived in free territory
Black Americans were not citizens; slavery was protected
Slavery was illegal in every state and territory
The Missouri Compromise was a valid use of federal power
questions.explain: The decision declared that people of African descent could not be US citizens and that the Missouri Compromise was unconstitutional.

questions.q: Who wrote the majority opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford?
questions.explain: Taney, a Maryland native, held that Black people were not citizens under the Constitution.

questions.q: Dred Scott sued for his freedom because he had lived in what places?
options: Free territory and a free state
The District of Columbia and Maryland
questions.explain: Scott had lived in Illinois and in the Wisconsin Territory, where slavery was banned, before returning to Missouri.

questions.q: What was a political effect of the Dred Scott decision in the North?
options: It ended the sectional crisis over the territories
It bolstered Republican claims of a Slave Power
It united northern and southern Democrats
It gave the Whig Party new strength in the North
questions.explain: Northerners saw the ruling as proof that slaveholders aimed to nationalize slavery.

questions.q: Chief Justice Taney's ruling in Dred Scott said that the Fifth Amendment did what for slaveholders?
options: Required equal citizenship for all free people
Protected property rights in slaves in the territories
Guaranteed freedom to every enslaved person in a free state
Banned the importation of enslaved people from abroad
questions.explain: Taney said Congress could not deprive a citizen of property, which included slaves, without due process.

questions.q: The Lecompton Constitution was a proposed constitution for which territory?
questions.explain: The proslavery document was drafted without a fair vote, and Congress eventually sent it back to Kansas voters, who rejected it.

questions.q: Stephen Douglas broke with President Buchanan over which issue in 1857-1858?
questions.explain: Douglas opposed admitting Kansas under a constitution that did not reflect voters' wishes.

questions.q: The Panic of 1857 hit which region the hardest?
options: The North more than the South
The South more than the North
questions.explain: Railroad and bank failures hurt northern businesses, while the cotton economy recovered quickly, bolstering southern confidence.

questions.q: The 1858 debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas took place in which state?
questions.explain: The two candidates for the US Senate held seven debates across Illinois in 1858.

questions.q: In the Lincoln-Douglas debates, Lincoln argued that what was wrong about slavery?
options: That it violated the Fugitive Slave Act
That it was a moral wrong that should not spread
That it was unconstitutional where it existed
questions.explain: Lincoln said the nation could not endure 'half slave and half free' and that slavery should be placed on the path to extinction.

questions.q: In the Freeport Doctrine, Douglas said territories could keep slavery out by doing what?
options: Refusing to pass local laws to protect it
questions.explain: Douglas tried to reconcile popular sovereignty with Dred Scott, angering southern Democrats.

questions.q: Who won the 1858 Illinois Senate election?
options: Abraham Lincoln, who won by a narrow majority
John Breckinridge, who ran as a Southern Democrat
William Seward, who ran as a Republican
Stephen Douglas, though Lincoln became famous
questions.explain: The legislature chose Douglas, but the debates made Lincoln a national figure and positioned him for 1860.

questions.q: Lincoln's 'House Divided' speech of 1858 said that the nation would do what?
options: Abolish slavery by the end of 1860
Settle the issue by a new compromise
Be all one thing or all the other
questions.explain: He warned that a government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free.

questions.q: John Brown's 1859 raid targeted a federal arsenal at which location?
questions.explain: Brown hoped to seize weapons to arm enslaved people for an uprising.

questions.q: What happened to John Brown after the Harpers Ferry raid?
options: He escaped to Canada and lived there
He received a pardon from the governor
He was captured, tried, and hanged
He was killed during the raid
questions.explain: Brown was captured by US Marines and executed in December 1859.

questions.q: Which US Army officer led the Marines who captured John Brown at Harpers Ferry?
questions.explain: Lee, then a colonel on leave at Arlington House, was sent to Harpers Ferry; J.E.B. Stuart served as his volunteer aide.

questions.q: Why did John Brown's raid deepen sectional divisions?
options: It alarmed southerners while some northerners praised Brown
It ended the Fugitive Slave Act in the North
It united the North and South in anger at Brown
It proved the Underground Railroad was illegal
questions.explain: Reaction in the North, where many praised Brown as a martyr, convinced many southerners that the North threatened them.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass declined to join John Brown's plan for the raid at Harpers Ferry because he thought it would do what?
options: It would fail and bring harsh retaliation
It would waste the abolitionists' money
questions.explain: Douglass met Brown before the raid and warned the attack on a federal arsenal was a trap.

questions.q: The 1860 Democratic party split into northern and southern wings, nominating Stephen Douglas and which southerner?
questions.explain: Southern Democrats met separately and nominated Vice President Breckinridge of Kentucky.

questions.q: The Constitutional Union Party of 1860, led by John Bell, ran on what platform?
options: Calling for immediate abolition throughout the country
Supporting the secession of the Deep South
Preserving the Union without addressing slavery
questions.explain: The party's focus was avoiding the crisis by upholding the Constitution and the Union.

questions.q: Who won the presidential election of 1860?
questions.explain: Lincoln won with a majority of electoral votes entirely from northern states, without being on the ballot in most of the South.

questions.q: Abraham Lincoln won the 1860 election with what share of the popular vote?
questions.explain: A four-way race meant Lincoln won the Electoral College with roughly 40 percent of the popular vote.

questions.q: Which state was the first to secede from the Union after Lincoln's election?
questions.explain: South Carolina passed its ordinance of secession on December 20, 1860.

questions.q: The first group of states to secede, in the winter of 1860-1861, were mainly where?
questions.explain: Seven Deep South states left before Lincoln took office and formed the Confederacy in February 1861.

questions.q: Which compromise effort in 1860-1861 would have extended the Missouri Compromise line to the Pacific?
questions.explain: Senator John Crittenden's plan failed when Lincoln and Republicans refused to accept slavery's extension.

questions.q: Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens declared in the 1861 'Cornerstone Speech' that the new government rested on what?
options: The belief that slavery was Black people's natural condition
That states had a right to leave the Union at will
That free trade and low taxes were the Confederacy's goals
That the president should serve only a single term
questions.explain: Stephens plainly said slavery was the cornerstone of the Confederacy, showing the war's central cause in the Confederates' own words.

questions.q: Jefferson Davis became president of which new government in February 1861?
questions.explain: Delegates meeting in Montgomery, Alabama, chose Davis, a former US senator and secretary of war.

questions.q: In his first inaugural address in March 1861, Lincoln said he would do what regarding slavery where it already existed?
questions.explain: Lincoln said he had no purpose to interfere with slavery in the states where it existed but vowed to hold federal property.

questions.q: Lincoln closed his first inaugural address with an appeal to what?
questions.explain: He urged the South not to destroy the bonds of affection, hoping they would be 'touched by the better angels of our nature.'

questions.q: The Civil War began in April 1861 with the Confederate bombardment of which fort?
questions.explain: Confederate guns fired on the federal garrison in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, and Major Robert Anderson surrendered.

questions.q: After Fort Sumter, Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers. This pushed which states to secede?
options: Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina
questions.explain: The Upper South refused to fight fellow southern states and joined the Confederacy.

questions.q: The border states that allowed slavery but stayed in the Union were what?
questions.explain: Lincoln worked hard to keep these four slave states loyal, fearing that their loss would cripple the Union cause.

questions.q: Why was Maryland strategically vital to Washington, D.C., in 1861?
options: Its secession would have cut off Washington
Maryland held the Union's main weapons factory
Maryland had the nation's largest port and navy
Maryland had the only railroads in the region
questions.explain: Pro-Confederate mobs attacked Union troops in Baltimore, and Lincoln acted to keep Maryland in the Union.

questions.q: Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus in 1861. What was the immediate concern?
options: Stopping resistance to the draft in New York
Ending Native American uprisings in the West
Preventing sabotage of rail lines to Washington
questions.explain: Chief Justice Taney in Ex parte Merryman said only Congress could suspend the writ, but Lincoln persisted.

questions.q: The Union's overall strategic plan to strangle the Confederacy by blockade and control of rivers was known as what?
questions.explain: General Winfield Scott proposed a blockade and a campaign down the Mississippi to squeeze the South.

questions.q: The first major land battle of the Civil War, in July 1861, was fought near which Virginia stream?
questions.explain: Union forces were routed at First Bull Run (Manassas), ending hopes for a short war.

questions.q: Spectators from Washington came to watch First Bull Run. What does this show?
options: The war had little importance to civilians
Many expected a short, easy Union victory
The army was far larger than needed
questions.explain: Civilians picnicked near the battlefield, but the Union defeat showed the war would be long and costly.

questions.q: Which general took command of the Union Army of the Potomac in 1861 and built it into a disciplined force?
questions.explain: McClellan organized the army around Washington, but his caution frustrated Lincoln.

questions.q: Which Confederate general earned his nickname at First Bull Run when a fellow officer compared him to a stone wall?
questions.explain: General Barnard Bee supposedly said Jackson stood 'like a stone wall,' giving him the name 'Stonewall.'

questions.q: The Arlington estate across the Potomac from Washington belonged to whom before the Civil War?
options: The family of Robert E. Lee
The family of Ulysses S. Grant
questions.explain: The home, inherited through Lee's wife Mary Custis, was seized by Union forces in 1861 and later became a national cemetery.

questions.q: Freedman's Village at Arlington was established in 1863 to do what?
options: A prison for captured Confederate officers
A factory to make Union uniforms
Shelter and aid for freed people
questions.explain: The settlement on the Arlington estate sheltered thousands of freed people during the war and after.

questions.q: The Union naval blockade of Confederate ports aimed to do what?
options: Cut off the South's exports and imports
Win control of the Mississippi River
questions.explain: The blockade limited cotton exports and the supply of war materials, though many ships still slipped through.

questions.q: The USS Monitor and CSS Virginia fought at Hampton Roads in 1862. Why was the battle important?
options: It was the only naval battle of the war
It was the first clash of ironclad ships
It broke the Union blockade of the South
