It sank the entire Confederate fleet
questions.explain: The ships fought to a draw, but it showed iron-armored steam warships had changed naval warfare.

questions.q: Which Union general captured Forts Henry and Donelson in Tennessee in early 1862, demanding 'unconditional surrender'?
questions.explain: The victories opened the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers to Union forces and made Grant a hero.

questions.q: The Battle of Shiloh in April 1862 showed what about the war?
options: It would end within a few weeks
It would be decided by cavalry raids
That the war would be long and costly
It would be fought mostly at sea
questions.explain: More than 23,000 men were killed, wounded, or missing in two days, shocking both sides.

questions.q: Union capture of which Confederate city in April 1862 gave the North control of the mouth of the Mississippi River?
questions.explain: Admiral David Farragut's fleet took the South's largest city and port.

questions.q: Robert E. Lee took command of which Confederate army in 1862?
questions.explain: Lee replaced the wounded Joseph Johnston during the Peninsula Campaign and led the army until 1865.

questions.q: The Seven Days Battles of 1862 ended which Union effort?
options: Grant's campaign along the Tennessee River
questions.explain: Lee drove McClellan back from the outskirts of Richmond, ending the Peninsula Campaign and its threat to the Confederate capital.

questions.q: The Battle of Antietam in September 1862 was fought in which state?
questions.explain: Lee's first invasion of the North ended at Antietam Creek near Sharpsburg.

questions.q: Antietam is remembered as what?
options: The first major battle of the war
The bloodiest day in US military history
The final battle of the war
A decisive Confederate victory in the North
questions.explain: About 23,000 casualties occurred in one day in September 1862.

questions.q: Why was the Union victory at Antietam politically important?
options: It let Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation
It ended the war within a month
It gave the Confederates control of Maryland
It brought France into the war on the Union side
questions.explain: Lincoln had waited for a battlefield success so the announcement would not look desperate.

questions.q: Which two generals commanded the opposing armies at the Battle of Antietam?
options: Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee
William T. Sherman and Joseph Johnston
Robert E. Lee and George McClellan
questions.explain: Lee commanded the Confederates and McClellan led the Army of the Potomac.

questions.q: Lincoln removed McClellan from command in November 1862 mainly because McClellan had done what?
options: He did not pursue Lee after Antietam
He lost the battle at Antietam
He refused to fight at Bull Run
questions.explain: Lincoln was frustrated by McClellan's reluctance to advance and replaced him with Ambrose Burnside.

questions.q: The Union disaster at Fredericksburg in December 1862 came under which commander?
questions.explain: Burnside ordered costly frontal assaults on Marye's Heights, and Lee won a lopsided victory.

questions.q: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on what date?
questions.explain: Lincoln issued a preliminary version in September 1862 and the final proclamation on New Year's Day.

questions.q: The Emancipation Proclamation declared freedom for enslaved people where?
options: In every state of the Union
In the District of Columbia only
questions.explain: It did not free enslaved people in loyal border states or in parts of the Confederacy already under Union control.

questions.q: Lincoln justified the Emancipation Proclamation as what?
options: A military necessity as commander in chief
A statute passed by Congress in 1862
A constitutional amendment ratified by the states
A ruling of the Supreme Court
questions.explain: He used his war powers to free enslaved people in rebel areas as a measure to weaken the Confederacy.

questions.q: Which was a major effect of the Emancipation Proclamation on the war's purpose?
options: It ended the draft in the North
It made abolition a war aim and cooled European support
It turned the war into a fight over tariffs
It lifted the Union blockade of the South
questions.explain: With slavery now an explicit issue, Britain and France were less likely to recognize the Confederacy.

questions.q: The Emancipation Proclamation also allowed what?
options: The integration of white and Black regiments
The enrollment of Black men in the army and navy
The commissioning of women as army officers
The hiring of foreign mercenaries by the Union
questions.explain: It declared that freed men would be received into the armed services.

questions.q: Which regiment of Black soldiers, led by Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, attacked Fort Wagner in 1863?
questions.explain: The 54th's courageous assault on Fort Wagner in South Carolina helped end doubts about Black soldiers' courage.

questions.q: About how many Black men served in the Union Army and Navy during the Civil War?
questions.explain: Roughly one in ten Union soldiers and sailors was Black, though they were paid less at first and served in segregated units.

questions.q: Black soldiers in the Union Army initially received less pay than white soldiers. How was this resolved?
options: The pay gap was never changed
They received land grants in place of wages
questions.explain: After protests and refusals to accept lower pay, Congress equalized pay retroactively in 1864.

questions.q: Two of Frederick Douglass's sons served in which famous Black regiment?
questions.explain: Charles and Lewis Douglass enlisted, and Douglass helped recruit for the regiment.

questions.q: Robert Smalls became a Civil War hero in 1862 by doing what?
options: Taking a Confederate ship to Union lines
Leading a slave revolt in Louisiana
Building a Union fort in Virginia
Spying on Lee's army for the Union
questions.explain: Smalls, an enslaved pilot, took the ship Planter and his family to freedom and later served in Congress.

questions.q: What was the Union Army's policy toward escaped slaves who came to its lines early in the war, called by General Benjamin Butler?
options: Returning them to their owners under the Fugitive Slave Act
Sending them to colonies in Africa
Giving each family a farm in the North
Treating them as 'contraband of war' and keeping them
questions.explain: Butler's term at Fort Monroe let the army keep fugitives who had been used by the Confederate war effort.

questions.q: The Confiscation Acts passed by Congress in 1861-1862 declared what?
options: All Confederate property would be returned after the war
Enslaved people used by the Confederate military were free
Slavery was abolished in every territory
questions.explain: Congress began using wartime power to free enslaved people who aided the rebellion.

questions.q: Congress abolished slavery in the District of Columbia in April 1862 with what feature?
options: A gradual schedule over ten years
questions.explain: The District of Columbia Compensated Emancipation Act freed about 3,000 people and paid owners up to $300 each.

questions.q: Which date is celebrated as Emancipation Day in Washington, D.C., marking the 1862 abolition of slavery in the District?
questions.explain: Lincoln signed the act on April 16, 1862, and the day is a DC holiday.

questions.q: The Union disaster at Chancellorsville in May 1863 was Lee's masterpiece but cost the South which leader?
questions.explain: Jackson was accidentally shot by Confederate soldiers and died of complications days later.

questions.q: What was the main goal of the Union's Vicksburg campaign?
options: Capture Richmond and end the war
Take Atlanta and cut Southern railroads
questions.explain: Capturing the fortress city would split the Confederacy east and west.

questions.q: Grant's victory at Vicksburg ended on what date, near that of Gettysburg?
questions.explain: The surrender of Vicksburg came the day after the Gettysburg fighting ended.

questions.q: The Battle of Gettysburg took place in which state?
questions.explain: Lee's second invasion of the North ended in defeat there in July 1863.

questions.q: Who commanded the Union forces at Gettysburg?
questions.explain: George G. Meade commanded the Union Army of the Potomac at Gettysburg. He had replaced Joseph Hooker just three days before the battle began.

questions.q: Gettysburg's final day featured a Confederate assault on the Union center known as what?
questions.explain: Pickett's Charge on July 3, 1863, sent thousands of Confederates against the Union center on Cemetery Ridge. Its failure ended Lee's invasion of the North.

questions.q: Why is Gettysburg often called a turning point of the war?
options: The Union gave up Washington and moved the capital
The Confederacy won recognition from Britain
Lee's invasion failed and his losses were severe
Lee surrendered his army to Meade
questions.explain: Afterward the Confederates remained mostly on the defensive.

questions.q: Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address in November 1863 at the dedication of what?
options: A national cemetery for Union soldiers
A new state capital for Pennsylvania
questions.explain: The ceremony consecrated the cemetery for the soldiers who died in the battle.

questions.q: The Gettysburg Address begins with what famous phrase?
options: 'Government of the people, by the people'
questions.explain: Lincoln dated the nation's birth to the Declaration of Independence of 1776.

questions.q: In the Gettysburg Address, Lincoln said the nation was 'dedicated to the proposition' that what?
questions.explain: He tied the war's purpose to the equality principle in the Declaration of Independence.

questions.q: What did Lincoln call for in the closing lines of the Gettysburg Address?
options: A negotiated peace with the Confederacy
An immediate end to slavery by executive order
A 'new birth of freedom' for the nation
Revenge on the South for the war
questions.explain: The brief speech reframed the war as a test of democratic self-government.

questions.q: Who was the main speaker at the Gettysburg cemetery dedication, giving a two-hour oration before Lincoln?
questions.explain: Everett, a famous orator, spoke for two hours; Lincoln spoke for about two minutes.

questions.q: The Union Army relied on conscription starting in March 1863. What provision caused anger?
options: Women were drafted into the army
Black men were exempt from service
Wealthy men could hire a substitute
questions.explain: The Enrollment Act allowed buying out of the draft for $300, fueling charges of a rich man's war and a poor man's fight.

questions.q: The New York City draft riots of July 1863 included what?
options: Mob attacks on Black residents and officials
A strike by dockworkers over wages
A mutiny aboard a navy ship in the harbor
questions.explain: Mobs, largely made up of poor workers angry about the draft, attacked Black New Yorkers and burned buildings.

questions.q: Copperheads in the North were what?
options: Radical abolitionists who wanted harsher war aims
Northern Democrats who urged peace with the South
questions.explain: Critics called these Peace Democrats 'Copperheads'; their leader Clement Vallandigham was exiled to the Confederacy.

questions.q: To help pay for the war, the federal government issued paper currency that was unredeemable in gold. What were these notes called?
questions.explain: The Legal Tender Act of 1862 authorized the greenbacks, which helped pay war costs.

questions.q: The National Banking Acts of 1863-1864 did what?
options: Rechartered the Second Bank of the United States
Abolished paper money in the North
Created national banks and a uniform currency
Gave state banks full control of currency
questions.explain: The acts helped sell war bonds and created a more uniform banking system.

questions.q: The first federal income tax in US history was enacted in 1861-1862 for what reason?
options: To pay for Reconstruction after the war
questions.explain: Congress also raised tariffs and excise taxes to fund the army and navy.

questions.q: The Morrill Land-Grant Act of 1862 supported what?
options: Colleges of agriculture and mechanical arts
questions.explain: The Morrill Act gave states federal land to sell to fund colleges teaching agriculture and mechanical arts. Many state universities began as land-grant colleges.

questions.q: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered settlers what?
options: Free passage on a railroad to the West
160 acres of public land after farming it for five years
A free set of farm tools and seed
questions.explain: Settlers could claim 160 acres and own it after five years of residence and improvement.

questions.q: The Pacific Railway Act of 1862 authorized which project?
questions.explain: The Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines were chartered, finished in 1869.

questions.q: The first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869 at which place?
questions.explain: The Golden Spike joined the Union Pacific and Central Pacific tracks.

questions.q: What technology allowed Union commanders to coordinate armies quickly during the war?
questions.explain: Telegraph lines linked Washington to field armies, letting Lincoln follow events and send orders.

questions.q: Union forces used what aircraft for reconnaissance during the war?
questions.explain: Thaddeus Lowe's Union Army Balloon Corps observed Confederate positions in 1861-1863.

questions.q: Clara Barton, remembered for aiding wounded soldiers, later founded what?
questions.explain: She delivered supplies to battlefields during the war and later established the American Red Cross in 1881.

questions.q: Where were many wounded soldiers treated in Washington during the war?
options: In converted public buildings and churches
Only on navy ships anchored in the Potomac
In field tents in southern Pennsylvania
In the private rooms of the White House
questions.explain: The city turned government buildings and churches into hospitals, and the poet Walt Whitman volunteered in them.

questions.q: Dr. Mary Walker, an Army surgeon in the Civil War, received which honor in 1865?
questions.explain: Walker was awarded the Medal of Honor by President Andrew Johnson for her wartime service as a surgeon.

questions.q: Women on both sides of the war often took on which responsibilities?
options: Commanding army units in the field
Serving as senators and cabinet members
Running farms and nursing the wounded
questions.explain: With men at war, many women managed households and economic life and served as nurses.

questions.q: Which general did Lincoln place in charge of all Union armies in March 1864?
questions.explain: Grant was promoted to lieutenant general and planned coordinated offensives against the Confederacy.

questions.q: Grant's 1864 Overland Campaign in Virginia was marked by what?
options: A series of quick, bloodless victories
A long pause with no major battles
A campaign fought mostly by the navy
questions.explain: The Wilderness, Spotsylvania, and Cold Harbor battles cost tens of thousands of casualties on both sides.

questions.q: The long Union siege of Petersburg, Virginia, aimed to do what?
options: Cut the rail lines feeding Richmond
questions.explain: Petersburg was a rail hub supplying the Confederate capital.

questions.q: Which Union general captured Atlanta in September 1864?
questions.explain: William T. Sherman captured Atlanta in September 1864. The victory lifted Northern morale and boosted Lincoln's chances in the November election.

questions.q: Why did the fall of Atlanta help Lincoln win reelection in 1864?
options: It ended the draft in the North
It led to the capture of Richmond
It freed all remaining enslaved people
It showed the war was being won
questions.explain: Before Atlanta, many feared Lincoln would lose; afterward his position strengthened.

questions.q: Who was Lincoln's Democratic opponent in 1864?
questions.explain: McClellan ran on a platform calling the war a failure but personally supported continuing it.

questions.q: Lincoln's 1864 running mate, who was a Southern Democrat loyal to the Union, was whom?
questions.explain: The National Union ticket balanced the Republican Lincoln with a Tennessee Democrat.

questions.q: Sherman's 'March to the Sea' in late 1864 ended at which Georgia city?
questions.explain: Sherman's army destroyed railroads and supplies, presenting Savannah to Lincoln as a Christmas gift.

questions.q: What was the purpose of Sherman's 'total war' strategy?
options: To take land to give to freed families
To win recognition from European powers
To wreck the South's ability to fight
questions.explain: His army destroyed railroads, crops, and property to weaken Confederate morale and supply.

questions.q: Special Field Order No. 15, issued by Sherman in January 1865, set aside what for freed families?
options: Free passage to Liberia for any freedperson who wished to go
Federal wages for freedpeople working on plantations
Government-built schools in every Southern county
questions.explain: The order is the basis of the phrase 'forty acres and a mule,' though President Johnson later reversed the policy.

questions.q: The Thirteenth Amendment, passed by Congress in January 1865, did what?
options: Gave Black men the right to vote
Abolished slavery in the United States
Ended racial segregation in public places
questions.explain: It banned slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment for a crime.

questions.q: Which house of Congress failed to reach the two-thirds vote on the Thirteenth Amendment in June 1864, leading Lincoln to press for its passage in early 1865?
questions.explain: The Senate passed the amendment in 1864 but the House fell short of two-thirds until January 31, 1865.

questions.q: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in what year?
questions.explain: It became part of the Constitution in December 1865 after three-fourths of states ratified.

questions.q: In his second inaugural address in March 1865, Lincoln urged the nation to proceed with 'malice toward none' and what?
questions.explain: He pledged to bind up the nation's wounds and care for those who had borne the battle.

questions.q: In his second inaugural address, what did Lincoln say about slavery's role in the war?
options: That it was somehow the cause of the war
That it was a side issue next to tariffs
That it had ended before the fighting began
That it was a matter only for the courts
questions.explain: Lincoln said the enslaved population was a 'peculiar and powerful interest' that 'was, somehow, the cause of the war,' and suggested the conflict might be divine judgment.

questions.q: At the White House reception after Lincoln's second inauguration, how did Frederick Douglass describe the inaugural address to Lincoln?
options: As too harsh toward the South
questions.explain: Douglass, who had been briefly turned away at the door, told Lincoln the speech was a sacred effort, and Lincoln said he valued Douglass's opinion.

questions.q: Richmond, the Confederate capital, fell to Union forces in what month of 1865?
questions.explain: Lee evacuated Petersburg and Richmond in early April, and Union troops entered the city on April 3.

questions.q: Robert E. Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant at which Virginia location?
questions.explain: The surrender on April 9, 1865, effectively ended the war in the east.

questions.q: What generous terms did Grant offer Lee's army at Appomattox?
options: Soldiers could go home with horses and keep property
They would be held as prisoners of war
They would pay reparations to the Union
They would be sent west to garrison forts
questions.explain: Grant also provided rations, setting a tone of reconciliation.

questions.q: On April 14, 1865, Lincoln attended a performance at Ford's Theatre. What play was being performed?
questions.explain: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln during the third act of the comedy.

questions.q: Who assassinated Abraham Lincoln?
questions.explain: Booth, an actor and Confederate sympathizer, shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre.

questions.q: After Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre, where was he taken?
options: The White House, a few blocks away
A boardinghouse across the street from the theater
The Capitol, where Lincoln's body would lie in state
A military hospital on the Potomac
questions.explain: Lincoln died in the Petersen House on the morning of April 15, 1865, never regaining consciousness.

questions.q: Which young Army surgeon was the first physician to reach Lincoln in the presidential box and tend his wound?
questions.explain: Charles Leale, a 23-year-old Army assistant surgeon in the audience, pushed through the crowd to the presidential box and kept Lincoln breathing until he could be moved.

questions.q: Booth's conspiracy also targeted which other officials on the night of April 14?
options: Secretary of War Edwin Stanton and General Grant
Treasury Secretary Salmon Chase and Edwin Stanton
Chief Justice Roger Taney and William Seward
Secretary of State Seward and Vice President Johnson
questions.explain: Lewis Powell badly wounded Seward, but the attempt on Johnson was never carried out.

questions.q: What happened to John Wilkes Booth after the assassination?
options: He was shot in Virginia on April 26
He escaped to Europe and lived there
He was convicted and hanged in Washington
questions.explain: Union troops cornered Booth in a tobacco barn near Port Royal, Virginia, and he was shot on April 26, 1865. He died a few hours later.

questions.q: The eight people tried for the Lincoln assassination conspiracy were tried by what kind of court?
questions.explain: Four were hanged in July 1865, including Mary Surratt, the first woman executed by the federal government.

questions.q: Mary Surratt was convicted because her boardinghouse had been used for what?
questions.explain: Her Washington boardinghouse was where Booth and others planned; her conviction remains debated.

questions.q: After Lincoln lay in state in Washington, his funeral train carried his body home to which city for burial?
questions.explain: Lincoln's funeral train largely retraced his 1861 route, with mourning crowds along the way.

questions.q: In what part of the US Capitol did Lincoln's body lie in state in April 1865?
questions.explain: His catafalque was placed beneath the dome while thousands paid respects.

questions.q: The Capitol's cast-iron dome was built during the Civil War. Under whose direction was it constructed?
options: Thomas U. Walter, with Lincoln's support
Benjamin Henry Latrobe, who had rebuilt it after 1814
Robert Mills, who designed the Treasury building
Pierre L'Enfant, who laid out the city
questions.explain: Lincoln insisted construction continue as a symbol that the Union would endure.

questions.q: The statue atop the Capitol dome, finished in 1863, is called what?
questions.explain: Thomas Crawford sculpted the bronze figure, and it was placed on the dome in December 1863.

questions.q: The Statue of Freedom's cast was made partly by whom?
options: Frederick Douglass, who had given a speech there
Philip Reid, an enslaved man who worked at the foundry
Henry Brown, who had mailed himself to freedom
Thomas Crawford, who designed the model for the statue
questions.explain: Reid helped cast the bronze statue's sections, and he was freed in 1862 when slavery ended in the District.

questions.q: The Washington Monument's construction was halted in the 1850s in part because of what?
options: Know-Nothings took over the memorial society
The quarry ran out of marble of the right color
A fire destroyed the monument's foundation
A dispute over its design stopped the architect
questions.explain: The society's takeover, and financial trouble, stopped work at about 150 feet until the 1870s.

questions.q: How did the Civil War affect the Washington Monument?
options: It was completed in time for Lincoln's inauguration
Work was halted and the unfinished shaft stood for years
It was destroyed by Confederate artillery
It was moved to a new site on the Potomac
questions.explain: The unfinished stump stood until Congress funded completion in the 1870s; the monument opened in 1888.

questions.q: A noticeable color change halfway up the Washington Monument reflects what?
options: Weathering from the Potomac River's damp climate
A halt in building and a new marble supply
Fire damage from the Civil War
A new architect's different taste in stone
questions.explain: Work stopped from the 1850s until 1879, and the later stone came from a different quarry.

questions.q: Reconstruction refers to the period after the Civil War when the nation worked to do what?
options: Readmit the South and define freedpeople's rights
Settle the western lands and build railroads
Fight a war against Spain in the Caribbean
questions.explain: Reconstruction (1865-1877) dealt with restoring the Union and the place of formerly enslaved people in it.

questions.q: Lincoln's Ten Percent Plan for Reconstruction offered to readmit a state when what happened?
options: A tenth of its land was given to freedpeople
A tenth of 1860 voters took an oath and slavery ended
A tenth of its soldiers surrendered to Union forces
It paid a ten percent tax on cotton
questions.explain: The 1863 plan was lenient, aiming to encourage Southern Unionists and speed restoration.

questions.q: Radical Republicans in Congress opposed Lincoln's Ten Percent Plan because they thought it did what?
options: They thought it was too harsh toward the South
They believed it required redistribution of land
They believed it denied statehood forever
It was too lenient toward former Confederates
questions.explain: Congress passed the stricter Wade-Davis Bill in 1864; Lincoln pocket-vetoed it.

questions.q: The Wade-Davis Bill of 1864 would have required what share of white men in a state to swear loyalty before readmission?
questions.explain: Lincoln's pocket veto left Reconstruction policy unsettled when he died.

questions.q: The Freedmen's Bureau, created in 1865, did what?
options: Ran the Union army's supply service
Provided food, schools, and legal aid to freedpeople
Set tariff rates for Southern ports
questions.explain: The agency operated within the War Department, and it helped found schools and negotiate labor contracts.

questions.q: Who led the Freedmen's Bureau as commissioner?
questions.explain: Howard, a Union general, later helped found Howard University in Washington, D.C.

questions.q: Howard University in Washington, D.C., was chartered in 1867 to provide what?
options: Training for immigrant lawyers and clerks
questions.explain: It was named for Oliver O. Howard, who helped establish it with Freedmen's Bureau support.

questions.q: Who became president after Lincoln's death?
questions.explain: Johnson, a former Tennessee senator and Unionist Democrat, took the oath in the hotel room where he was staying.

questions.q: Andrew Johnson's Reconstruction plan was marked by what?
options: A plan to divide plantations among freedpeople
A guarantee of voting rights for Black men
Military rule across the entire South
Quick pardons and few conditions for readmission
questions.explain: He required states to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment and void secession but otherwise allowed white Southern leaders to regain power.

questions.q: Black Codes passed by Southern states after 1865 were meant to do what?
options: Limit the freedom and labor of freedpeople
Grant freedmen the vote in local elections
questions.explain: The codes limited where Black Southerners could work, travel, and own property and punished 'vagrancy' with forced labor.

questions.q: Which Black Code provision let officials arrest unemployed freedpeople and hire them out?
questions.explain: Vagrancy and apprenticeship laws pushed many Black workers back into plantation labor.

questions.q: Northern reaction to the Black Codes and the election of former Confederate leaders to Congress did what?
options: It strengthened Johnson's hold on policy
It led to a second civil war
questions.explain: Congress refused to seat the Southern delegations and formed the Joint Committee on Reconstruction.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 declared what?
options: Segregation in public places was legal
Women could vote in federal elections
Nearly all people born in the US were citizens
questions.explain: It was the first federal law defining citizenship, covering nearly all people born in the US (not Native Americans outside taxation), and passed over Johnson's veto.

questions.q: How did Congress respond to Johnson's 1866 vetoes of the Civil Rights Act and the revised Freedmen's Bureau bill of July 1866?
options: It accepted them and rewrote the bills
It impeached him over the vetoes at once
It overrode them with two-thirds majorities
It asked the Supreme Court to decide
questions.explain: Congress overrode both vetoes with two-thirds majorities (an earlier February 1866 Freedmen's Bureau veto had been sustained); the Civil Rights Act override in April 1866 was the first major law passed over a presidential veto.

questions.q: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, did what?
options: Gave women the right to vote nationwide
Ended slavery throughout the United States
Banned racial limits on voting in all states
questions.explain: It overturned Dred Scott by making all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens.

questions.q: Which clause of the Fourteenth Amendment states that no state shall deny any person 'equal protection of the laws'?
questions.explain: The clause became the basis for many later civil rights decisions.

questions.q: The Fourteenth Amendment reduced a state's representation in Congress if it did what?
options: Failed to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment
Denied the vote to adult male citizens
questions.explain: This provision was meant to push Southern states toward allowing Black men to vote, though it was seldom enforced.

questions.q: The Fourteenth Amendment barred former Confederate officials from office. How could this be waived?
options: By a two-thirds vote of Congress
questions.explain: Section 3 let Congress remove the disqualification, and it did so for many former Confederates in 1872.

questions.q: The Reconstruction Acts of 1867 divided most of the former Confederacy into what?
questions.explain: Military commanders oversaw registration of voters, including Black men, and new state constitutions.

questions.q: The Reconstruction Acts required Southern states to do what to be readmitted?
options: Ratify the 14th Amendment and let Black men vote
Pay damages to Northern states for the war
Disband all state militias for a decade
Abolish the Democratic Party across the South
questions.explain: Congress required new state constitutions and ratification of the amendment.

questions.q: The Tenure of Office Act of 1867 limited the president's power to do what?
options: Command the army in the field
questions.explain: Congress passed it over Johnson's veto to protect Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, an ally of the Radicals.

questions.q: Andrew Johnson became the first president to be what?
options: Impeached by the House of Representatives
Elected by the House of Representatives
Removed from office by the Supreme Court
questions.explain: The House impeached Andrew Johnson in February 1868, mainly for violating the Tenure of Office Act. The Senate acquitted him by a single vote.

questions.q: The immediate trigger for Johnson's impeachment in 1868 was his attempt to do what?
options: Fire Secretary of War Edwin Stanton
questions.explain: Johnson's attempt to dismiss Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act led the House to vote for impeachment.

questions.q: What was the result of Johnson's Senate impeachment trial?
options: He was acquitted by one vote
questions.explain: The Senate fell one vote short of the two-thirds majority needed to convict.

questions.q: The Senate trial of Andrew Johnson was presided over by whom?
questions.explain: The Constitution calls for the chief justice to preside over a presidential impeachment trial.

questions.q: Which Republican senator was among those who voted to acquit Johnson, helping end the trial?
questions.explain: Ross of Kansas and several other Republicans voted not guilty, partly on concerns about the case and the successor.

questions.q: Which Radical Republican leader in the House was a driving force behind Johnson's impeachment?
questions.explain: Stevens of Pennsylvania pushed for strong Reconstruction measures and equal rights.

questions.q: The 1867 purchase of Alaska from Russia, negotiated by Secretary of State William Seward, was called by critics what?
questions.explain: Many thought the 7.2 million dollars spent on Alaska was wasteful, but the territory proved valuable.

questions.q: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, protected what right?
options: Voting rights regardless of race or past servitude
The right of women to vote in federal elections
The right to a jury trial in civil cases
The right to own property in every state
questions.explain: It banned denying the vote on account of race but did not address women or many indirect barriers.

questions.q: Which cause was left out of the Fifteenth Amendment, disappointing Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony?
questions.explain: Many women's rights activists were disappointed, and the movement split into two groups.

questions.q: Hiram Revels of Mississippi made history in 1870 as the first what?
options: Black member of the US Senate
questions.explain: Hiram Revels became the first Black member of the US Senate in 1870, representing Mississippi. His seat had last been held by Albert G. Brown, who left when Mississippi seceded.

questions.q: Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first what in 1870?
questions.explain: Rainey served until 1879 and was one of many Black men elected to Congress during Reconstruction.

questions.q: Blanche K. Bruce of Mississippi served as what?
options: The first Black governor of any state in the Union
The first Black senator to serve a full term
A general in the Union army
questions.explain: Bruce was elected in 1874 and presided over the Senate on one occasion.

questions.q: Black voters in the Reconstruction South mostly supported which party?
questions.explain: Black voters allied with white Unionists and Northern newcomers in Southern Republican governments.

questions.q: Southern white Republicans who supported Reconstruction were called what by their opponents?
questions.explain: Scalawag was a term used by opponents for white Southerners who cooperated with Republican governments.

questions.q: The term 'carpetbagger' described which group?
options: Freedmen who bought land from planters
Confederate officers who returned to politics
Settlers heading to the Western territories
questions.explain: Opponents used the term for newcomers they accused of exploiting the region; many were teachers, businessmen, and officials.

questions.q: Southern Reconstruction governments created what lasting improvements?
options: The elimination of all taxes in the South
The creation of a national church
questions.explain: Their constitutions established public schooling in much of the South and expanded access to the courts.

questions.q: The Ku Klux Klan was founded in 1865-1866 and used what methods?
options: Terror and violence against Black voters
questions.explain: The Klan began as a secret group in Tennessee and became a violent force trying to restore white control.

questions.q: The Enforcement Acts of 1870-1871, also called the Ku Klux Klan Acts, did what?
options: Banned the Democratic Party in Southern states
Disbanded state militias in the South
Made voter interference a federal crime
Gave land to freedpeople in the Black Belt
questions.explain: President Grant used the acts to prosecute Klan members in South Carolina and elsewhere.

questions.q: Which place saw a large 1873 massacre in which white paramilitaries killed many Black men defending a courthouse?
questions.explain: The Colfax massacre was among the deadliest incidents of Reconstruction violence.

questions.q: In United States v. Cruikshank (1876), the Supreme Court did what?
options: Upheld the Enforcement Acts in full
Limited federal prosecution of private violence
Ended the Ku Klux Klan's activity
questions.explain: The Court weakened enforcement of the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, a setback for Black voting rights.

questions.q: The Slaughter-House Cases (1873) narrowed the Fourteenth Amendment by what reasoning?
options: A ruling that ended the amendment's force
A narrow reading of national citizenship privileges
A decision banning state courts from civil rights cases
A reading that extended the amendment to corporations
questions.explain: The Court read the Privileges or Immunities Clause very narrowly, limiting its protective force.

questions.q: Many Black and white Southern farmers after the war ended up in what labor system?
questions.explain: Sharecroppers farmed land owned by others in return for a share of the crop.

questions.q: Why did sharecropping often trap families in debt?
options: Federal law required sharecroppers to stay in debt
Merchants charged high prices and interest on credit
Crops grown by sharecroppers had no market value
Farmers had to pay their taxes with their labor
questions.explain: The crop-lien system left many farmers owing more than they earned.

questions.q: Freedpeople wanted land after emancipation. What happened to the idea of redistributing Confederate land?
options: Land mostly returned to former owners
It was fully carried out across the South
It was ordered by the Supreme Court
It was approved by President Johnson
questions.explain: Johnson pardoned ex-Confederates and restored property, leaving most freedpeople without land.

questions.q: Which institutions did Black Southerners build during Reconstruction as centers of community life?
questions.explain: Independent Black churches, schools, and mutual aid societies gained strength after emancipation.

questions.q: Ulysses S. Grant was elected president in 1868. His slogan 'Let us have peace' reflected what?
options: A wish to end conflict while enforcing Reconstruction
A plan to abandon Reconstruction and leave the South alone
A call for higher federal taxes to pay the war debt
A desire to begin a war with Spain over Cuba
questions.explain: Grant, the Union hero, supported the Reconstruction amendments but his administration was plagued by scandals.

questions.q: The 'Crédit Mobilier' scandal of the 1870s involved what?
options: Fraud in the collection of federal whiskey taxes
Land fraud in the settlement of Florida
Bribery tied to the building of the Union Pacific Railroad
Bribes paid to win the purchase of Alaska
questions.explain: Company shares were given to congressmen to avoid investigation of overcharging.

questions.q: The Whiskey Ring scandal under Grant involved what?
options: A plot to sell Alaska to Britain for a profit
Bribery of congressmen in building a railroad
Officials who defrauded the government of liquor tax revenue
An attempt to pack the Supreme Court with allies
questions.explain: Distillers and revenue officials stole taxes; Grant's secretary Orville Babcock was implicated but acquitted.

questions.q: The Panic of 1873 began when what happened?
options: The bank Jay Cooke and Company failed
The Bank of the United States closed
questions.explain: Overbuilding of railroads and speculation led to bank failures and a long depression.

questions.q: The Coinage Act of 1873, which dropped silver as a coin, was later called what by critics?
questions.explain: Farmers and debtors wanting inflation blamed the act for tightening money.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1875 aimed to do what?
options: Give land to freedpeople across the South
Create a federal system of public schools
Guarantee equal access to inns and theaters
Ban the Ku Klux Klan in every state
questions.explain: The Supreme Court struck down its main provisions in the Civil Rights Cases of 1883.

questions.q: Which Massachusetts senator, nearly killed in 1856, championed the Civil Rights Act that passed after his death in 1874?
questions.explain: Sumner pushed for the bill for years, and Congress passed it in 1875 in his memory.

questions.q: The presidential election of 1876 pitted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes against which Democrat?
questions.explain: Tilden won the popular vote, but disputed electoral votes in three Southern states decided the outcome.

questions.q: Disputed returns in 1876 came from which three Southern states?
questions.explain: Both parties claimed victory there, and Congress created an Electoral Commission to decide.

questions.q: The Electoral Commission of 1877 was made up of members from which groups?
options: Members of Congress and justices of the Supreme Court
Senators only, chosen by the Senate majority
Members of Grant's cabinet and the vice president
State governors from the disputed states
questions.explain: Fifteen members were drawn from the House, Senate, and Supreme Court, and it awarded all disputed votes to Hayes.

questions.q: The Compromise of 1877 resolved the election dispute by doing what?
options: Hayes became president and federal troops left the South
Tilden became president after a recount of Florida's ballots
A new national election was held in 1877
The Electoral College was abolished by amendment
questions.explain: Democrats accepted Hayes's win after promises of troop withdrawal and Southern internal improvements.

questions.q: What was the main effect of the Compromise of 1877 on the South?
options: It restored slavery in the South under new state laws
It ended federal Reconstruction in the South
It expanded Black voting rights through new federal laws
It created new military districts across the South
questions.explain: Withdrawal of troops allowed Redeemers to take over and Black rights gradually eroded.

questions.q: Southern white Democrats who regained control of state governments after Reconstruction were called what?
questions.explain: They claimed to 'redeem' the South from Republican rule, then cut taxes and spending on schools.

questions.q: What name was given to the thousands of Black Southerners who migrated to Kansas in 1879 to escape violence and poverty?
questions.explain: The Exodusters, encouraged by figures like Benjamin 'Pap' Singleton, sought land and safety on the Plains.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass was appointed to which post by President Hayes in 1877?
options: Secretary of State under President Grant
Senator from New York after Reconstruction
Marshal of the District of Columbia
Ambassador to France for two terms
questions.explain: Douglass served as US marshal for the District of Columbia and later as recorder of deeds.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass later served as US minister to which country?
questions.explain: President Benjamin Harrison appointed Douglass minister resident and consul general to Haiti in 1889.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass's home in Washington, D.C., is known by what name?
questions.explain: Douglass bought Cedar Hill in Anacostia in 1877, moved in during 1878, and lived there until his death in 1895.

questions.q: In what neighborhood of Washington is Douglass's home located?
questions.explain: The home overlooks the Anacostia River and is now a National Historic Site.

questions.q: Douglass gave a famous speech at the 1876 dedication of the Freedmen's Monument in Washington. What did he say about Lincoln?
options: That Lincoln was an enemy of Black Americans throughout his life
That Lincoln had played no part in ending slavery
That Lincoln was devoted to white interests yet deserved honor
That Lincoln should be remembered only as a Southern sympathizer
questions.explain: Douglass said Black Americans were 'at best only his step-children,' yet he honored Lincoln's role in ending slavery.

questions.q: The Emancipation Memorial in Lincoln Park in Washington was funded largely by whom?
options: The federal government through an act of Congress
Wealthy Southern donors seeking to honor Lincoln
Formerly enslaved people, who donated money
questions.explain: Charlotte Scott, a freedwoman, gave the first five dollars, and Black veterans and others funded the monument.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Cases (1883) decision came after Reconstruction and did what?
options: Upheld the Civil Rights Act of 1875 in every provision
Banned segregation in schools across the South
Struck down the 1875 act's ban on private discrimination
Created the system of Jim Crow laws by statute
questions.explain: The Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment did not cover private discrimination.

questions.q: The telegraph, invented by Samuel F. B. Morse, sent its first long-distance message from Washington to Baltimore in 1844. What did it say?
questions.explain: Morse sent the biblical phrase from the U.S. Capitol to Baltimore on May 24, 1844, opening the age of instant communication.

questions.q: Where in the Capitol did Morse send the 1844 telegraph message?
options: The Capitol Rotunda beneath the dome
The Senate Chamber on the north wing
Statuary Hall in the old House chamber
questions.explain: He sent the message from the Capitol to Baltimore over an experimental line paid for by Congress.

questions.q: The Treaty of Washington (1871) with Britain settled which dispute?
options: A dispute over the Canadian boundary near Maine
Control of the Oregon Country's coast
Fishing rights near the Hawaiian Islands
Claims over Confederate cruisers like the Alabama
questions.explain: An arbitration panel awarded the United States 15.5 million dollars for damage caused by British-built raiders.

questions.q: Which policy of the 1860s-1870s sought to move Plains Native nations onto reservations and assimilate them?
options: The policy of Indian Removal to the west
The idea of Manifest Destiny across the continent
The policy of isolation from European powers
questions.explain: After the Civil War, the government and army pushed Plains nations onto reservations.

questions.q: At the Battle of Little Bighorn in 1876, who led the 7th Cavalry?
questions.explain: Custer and his men were defeated by a large force of Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors.

questions.q: The Lakota leaders who helped win at Little Bighorn included which pair?
questions.explain: The Native victory led to intensified US military efforts, and the Lakota were later forced onto reservations.

questions.q: The Sand Creek Massacre of 1864 took place in which territory?
questions.explain: Colorado militia attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho camp, killing many, mostly women, children, and elderly people.

questions.q: The Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) was notable because it did what?
options: Created Indian Territory for the removed southeastern nations
Recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation
Opened the Black Hills to mining companies and settlers
Ended the Civil War in the Southwest territories
questions.explain: The US later broke the treaty after gold was found in the Black Hills in 1874.

questions.q: Black cavalry regiments in the Army's Western campaigns were nicknamed what by Native Americans?
questions.explain: The 9th and 10th Cavalry, formed in 1866, were Black units that served on the frontier.

questions.q: Abraham Lincoln was born in which state?
questions.explain: Lincoln was born in a log cabin in Kentucky in 1809 and grew up in Indiana and Illinois.

questions.q: Abraham Lincoln's early career before politics included work as what?
options: A newspaper publisher in New York
questions.explain: Largely self-taught, Lincoln became a lawyer in Springfield and served in the Illinois legislature.

questions.q: Lincoln served one term in the US House of Representatives from 1847 to 1849 as a member of which party?
questions.explain: Lincoln served one term in the House as a Whig from Illinois, from 1847 to 1849. He joined the new Republican Party in 1856.

questions.q: Lincoln's cabinet included his former rivals Seward, Chase, and Bates. This has been described as what?
questions.explain: Lincoln brought leading political opponents into his cabinet to unite the party and the Union.

questions.q: Who served as Lincoln's Secretary of State and negotiated the Alaska purchase under Andrew Johnson?
questions.explain: Seward helped keep Britain and France out of the war and was nearly killed on the night Lincoln was shot.

questions.q: Who served as Lincoln's Secretary of the Treasury, helped create national banks, and later became chief justice?
questions.explain: Chase oversaw Civil War finance and was named chief justice in 1864.

questions.q: Which Secretary of War organized the Union war effort under Lincoln from 1862 and was at the president's bedside when he died?
questions.explain: Stanton replaced Simon Cameron in January 1862 and later stayed in office to clash with President Johnson over Reconstruction.

questions.q: The Trent Affair of 1861 nearly brought which nation into the war?
questions.explain: A Union ship seized two Confederate diplomats from a British vessel; Lincoln released them to avoid war.

questions.q: Which factor helped keep Britain from recognizing the Confederacy despite its need for cotton?
options: A Union promise to cut tariffs sharply on British manufactured goods
A French threat of war if Britain recognized the Confederacy
Antislavery opinion and new cotton sources made intervention unattractive
A secret Lincoln offer to give Canada to Britain for support
questions.explain: Emancipation made the war about slavery, and Britain had stockpiles and alternate suppliers of cotton.

questions.q: What was the main way Confederate leaders paid for the war?
options: Collecting large tariffs at Southern ports
Printing paper money, causing severe inflation
questions.explain: With the blockade cutting revenue, the Confederacy relied on money printing and fast inflation hurt civilians.

questions.q: Why did the Confederacy's 'King Cotton' diplomacy fail?
options: Cotton prices collapsed in Liverpool after the war began
The North shipped all its cotton abroad before the war
France controlled shipping in the Atlantic and blocked Britain
Britain had stockpiles and found other cotton sources
questions.explain: The Confederate hope that cotton shortages would force British recognition proved wrong.

questions.q: Southern states that seceded gave reasons in their declarations. A central cause they cited was what?
questions.explain: Mississippi's declaration said its position was 'thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery,' and others made similar statements.

questions.q: What prompted the Confederate decision to attack Fort Sumter in April 1861?
options: Lincoln's decision to resupply the fort
A Union invasion of South Carolina
questions.explain: Lincoln sent supplies only, leaving it to the Confederacy to decide whether to fire the first shot.

questions.q: West Virginia was created in 1863 when what happened?
options: Western counties loyal to the Union separated from Virginia
The Confederacy gave land to the Union in a peace treaty
Congress redrew the borders of Virginia without its consent
Maryland ceded its western counties to the Union
questions.explain: Unionist western Virginians formed a new state and Lincoln admitted it in June 1863.

questions.q: Which two Confederate strongholds on the Mississippi were the last to fall in July 1863, giving the Union control of the river?
questions.explain: After they fell in July 1863, the Union controlled the whole river.

questions.q: The Battle of Chickamauga in September 1863 was a Confederate victory in which state?
questions.explain: Fought near Chickamauga Creek in northern Georgia, it was one of the bloodiest battles of the war.

questions.q: Grant's victory at Chattanooga in November 1863 opened the way for what?
questions.explain: Grant's victory at Chattanooga secured Tennessee for the Union and opened the gateway to Georgia, setting up Sherman's Atlanta campaign in 1864.

questions.q: Why did Confederate General John Bell Hood evacuate Atlanta in September 1864?
options: He ran out of recruits to surrender
Sherman had cut his last railroad supply line
questions.explain: After Union forces cut the Macon railroad, Hood abandoned the city and Sherman occupied it on September 2.

questions.q: Sheridan's destruction of crops and barns in the Shenandoah Valley in autumn 1864 was meant to do what?
options: Capture the Confederate capital at Richmond
Destroy the valley's food supplies that fed Lee's army
Cut Union supply lines in western Maryland
Defend Washington from a Confederate attack
questions.explain: Sheridan's burning of crops and barns was a major part of the Union plan to end the war.

questions.q: Confederate General Jubal Early's 1864 raid reached the outskirts of Washington at which place?
questions.explain: Lincoln watched the fighting from Fort Stevens on July 12, 1864, and came under Confederate sharpshooter fire; Early's raid then withdrew.

questions.q: Union forces used what new weapon type that fired rapid shots, like the Spencer repeating rifle?
questions.explain: Repeaters boosted firepower, though most infantry still carried single-shot rifled muskets.

questions.q: The rifled musket's greater accuracy meant what for tactics?
options: Armies chose to fight at night
questions.explain: Defenders could hit attackers at long range, making charges extremely costly.

questions.q: Which prison camp in Georgia became infamous for its deadly conditions?
questions.explain: About 13,000 Union prisoners died there, and its commander Henry Wirz was executed after the war.

questions.q: The Fort Pillow Massacre in April 1864 involved what?
options: A Union victory over Forrest's cavalry in western Tennessee
A prisoner exchange arranged by both armies
Confederate troops killed Black soldiers who surrendered
A slave revolt against a nearby plantation
questions.explain: The event outraged the North and shaped the Union debate over treatment of Black soldiers.

questions.q: What inscription appears on the walls of the Lincoln Memorial's interior chambers?
options: The Emancipation Proclamation and the Constitution
The Gettysburg Address and the second inaugural address
questions.explain: Texts of the two speeches are carved on the north and south walls of the memorial.

questions.q: The Lincoln Memorial, designed by Henry Bacon, was modeled on what?
questions.explain: The marble temple with 36 columns represents the states in the Union at Lincoln's death.

questions.q: How many Doric columns form the Lincoln Memorial's outer colonnade, one for each state in the Union at Lincoln's death?
questions.explain: The colonnade has 36 Doric columns, matching the 36 states in the Union when Lincoln died in 1865.

questions.q: Who sculpted the seated statue of Lincoln inside the Lincoln Memorial?
questions.explain: French's statue, carved in Georgia marble, was dedicated in 1922.

questions.q: What happened at Ford's Theatre after Lincoln's death in 1865?
options: It reopened as a thriving theater within a year
The government took it over and used it for offices
It became a military prison for Confederates
It was demolished to make room for a new hotel
questions.explain: Ford's Theatre was closed after the assassination and the government bought it; a floor collapse in 1893 killed workers.

questions.q: In 1893, a collapse inside the former Ford's Theatre, then a government office building, did what?
options: Burned the building to the ground
Collapsed the roof onto a crowded audience
Killed 22 clerks and injured many more
questions.explain: The June 1893 collapse of the federal office building killed 22 clerks; the site later became a museum and was restored as a theater.

questions.q: Lincoln's assassin, John Wilkes Booth, was from a well-known family of what?
questions.explain: His brother Edwin Booth was one of the best-known stage actors in America.

questions.q: Why did Booth want to harm Lincoln, according to his own writings and statements?
options: He wanted nothing but personal fame and fortune
He believed the Union should win the war
He opposed Lincoln's policies and backed the Confederacy
He was secretly working as a Union spy
questions.explain: Booth was outraged after hearing Lincoln support voting rights for some Black men days earlier.

questions.q: Before the assassination, Booth had planned to do what to Lincoln?
options: Poison him at a state dinner
Challenge him to a duel in Illinois
Ambush him on a trip to Springfield
Kidnap him in exchange for Confederate prisoners
questions.explain: The kidnapping plot gave way to murder after Lee's surrender and Richmond's fall.

questions.q: Who, as head of the Army's Bureau of Military Justice, directed the investigation and prosecution of the Lincoln assassination conspirators?
options: Joseph Holt, the Judge Advocate General
William Seward, the secretary of state
questions.explain: Holt oversaw the prosecution before the military commission.

questions.q: Dr. Samuel Mudd, who set Booth's broken leg, was convicted of conspiracy and sentenced to what?
options: Death by hanging with the others
Ten years' probation and a fine
Life in prison, though he was pardoned later
questions.explain: President Johnson pardoned him in 1869; his guilt is still debated.

questions.q: After Lincoln's death, Vice President Johnson had to deal with a Congress led by whom?
questions.explain: Radicals like Thaddeus Stevens and Charles Sumner pressed for stronger Reconstruction measures.

questions.q: Johnson's 1866 'Swing Around the Circle' speaking tour harmed him because it did what?
options: Featured angry exchanges with hecklers and hurt his image
Won him broad support in the Northern states
Led to his resignation as president
Improved Congress's view of his policies
questions.explain: The midterm elections that year gave Republicans a veto-proof majority.

questions.q: Which Union Navy hero from South Carolina later served in Congress during Reconstruction?
questions.explain: After seizing the Planter in 1862, Smalls became a pilot, ship captain, and later a congressman.

questions.q: In which year did Congress abolish the Freedmen's Bureau?
questions.explain: Congress abolished the Bureau in 1872; its education work had largely wound down in 1870, though many schools it helped found continued.

questions.q: Historically Black colleges founded after the Civil War include which of the following?
questions.explain: Freedmen's Bureau, churches, and missionary groups helped found schools such as Howard, Fisk, and Morehouse.

questions.q: In the 1868 election, Grant won despite violence against Black voters in the South because of what?
options: Grant swept every Southern state with white support
Southern white voters strongly backed him
Black votes in the South helped give him his popular-vote margin
President Johnson campaigned for him in the South
questions.explain: Black voters were crucial to Grant's margin, and this is one reason Republicans backed the Fifteenth Amendment.

questions.q: After Reconstruction, which devices let Southern states block Black voters without mentioning race?
questions.explain: Southern states later used these devices to disenfranchise Black voters without naming race.

questions.q: Which famous poem by Walt Whitman mourned Lincoln?
questions.explain: Whitman wrote of the captain who had won the voyage yet lay dead on the deck.

questions.q: Which Civil War photographer made some of the first widely viewed images of battle dead after Antietam?
options: Alexander Gardner, shown at Mathew Brady's gallery
questions.explain: Gardner's Antietam images were exhibited in Mathew Brady's New York gallery, shocking viewers with the war's reality.

questions.q: Photography in the Civil War era changed how Americans saw the war because it did what?
options: Replaced newspapers as the main source of news
Introduced color images of the battlefield
Brought realistic images of battle to the public
Allowed moving pictures of the fighting
questions.explain: Exhibitions and prints let civilians view the dead for the first time.

questions.q: The 'Battle Hymn of the Republic' lyrics were written after Julia Ward Howe visited Union camps near what city?
questions.explain: Howe heard soldiers singing 'John Brown's Body' and wrote new words to the same melody.

questions.q: Which song was a popular tribute to John Brown sung by Union soldiers?
questions.explain: Union soldiers sang it as they marched, and its melody became the base for the 'Battle Hymn.'

questions.q: Walt Whitman worked during the war as what?
options: A Union general in the Army of the Potomac
A volunteer nurse and writer in Washington hospitals
questions.explain: He visited wounded soldiers and wrote 'Drum-Taps' about the war.

questions.q: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 was passed during which president's term?
questions.explain: Monroe signed the compromise and the Missouri Constitution issues were resolved the next year.

questions.q: The 'market revolution' of the early 1800s was a shift toward what?
options: A shift toward commercial exchange from local self-sufficiency
A shift to a national barter system without money
A shift to plantation labor in northern states
A shift to government-owned industry and farms
questions.explain: Improved transportation and factories let farmers and workers sell to distant markets.

questions.q: The first successful American steam locomotive railroads in the 1830s were important because they did what?
options: Linked cities and farms with faster, year-round transport
Replaced the telegraph as the fastest communication
Put an immediate end to steamboat travel
Closed the canals within a few months
questions.explain: Rail lines, like the Baltimore and Ohio, grew rapidly and reshaped trade.

questions.q: Which early railroad, chartered in 1827, built a famous line connecting Baltimore with the West?
questions.explain: The B&O was the first major common-carrier railroad in the United States.

questions.q: How did the Erie Canal affect settlement in the Great Lakes region?
options: It stopped migration to the Great Lakes region
It brought migrants and farm output to the Old Northwest
It was used only to move military supplies
It ended farming in upstate New York
questions.explain: Canal shipping made it cheaper to send crops east and encouraged new towns.

questions.q: The factory system of the 1830s and 1840s led to the rise of what?
options: Minimum wage laws across New England
questions.explain: Workers' associations and strikes appeared as wages fell and hours stayed long.

questions.q: In Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842), the Massachusetts court ruled that what was legal?
options: Company stores run by factory owners
questions.explain: The decision recognized that workers could organize to seek better conditions.

questions.q: Which group made up many of the workers in early New England textile mills after the 1840s?
questions.explain: As Yankee mill girls left, immigrants filled many mill jobs at lower pay.

questions.q: Despite the expansion of democracy under Jackson, which groups were still mostly shut out of voting?
options: Women and most Black men, plus Native Americans
Wealthy men from the eastern states
questions.explain: Democratic expansion in this era was largely limited to white men.

questions.q: In the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830), which nation agreed to give up its lands in Mississippi?
questions.explain: The Choctaw were the first of the southeastern nations removed under the Indian Removal Act.

questions.q: The land to which Native nations were removed was called what?
questions.explain: Native nations forced out by removal were sent to Indian Territory, which lay mostly in present-day Oklahoma.

questions.q: Which president presided over the Trail of Tears removal of the Cherokee, enforcing the 1835 treaty?
questions.explain: Van Buren was president in 1838 when troops under General Winfield Scott rounded up the Cherokee.

questions.q: Why did settlers and the state of Georgia want Cherokee land?
options: To build railroads to the Pacific
To open ports on the Gulf Coast
Farmland, and gold found on Cherokee land
To build new forts along the Mississippi
questions.explain: Gold was found in northern Georgia in 1829, adding pressure to remove the Cherokee.

questions.q: The Mormon Church moved west to escape what?
options: Famine and crop failures in Illinois
Heavy taxes imposed by the state
questions.explain: Mobs and conflicts drove Latter-day Saints from Missouri and Illinois.

questions.q: The Liberty Party, formed in 1840, was notable for what?
options: Backing the Second Bank of the United States
questions.explain: The party was an early political voice for abolition, with James G. Birney as a candidate.

questions.q: The Underground Railroad's conductors included both Black and white abolitionists. Which Quaker helped many escape through Indiana?
questions.explain: Coffin, sometimes called the president of the Underground Railroad, aided thousands of freedom seekers.

questions.q: William Still, a Black abolitionist from Philadelphia, is known for what?
options: Writing the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
Recording the stories of fugitives in his book
Leading the Amistad revolt at sea
questions.explain: Still kept detailed records of those who passed through Philadelphia and published them in 1872.

questions.q: Which architect drew the original design for the Washington Monument, an obelisk surrounded by a circular colonnade?
questions.explain: Mills's 1845 plan called for a tall obelisk above a colonnaded base; the colonnade was dropped for lack of money, and the obelisk was built.

questions.q: Know-Nothing partisans took control of the Washington Monument society after what donated item disappeared in 1854?
options: A flag presented by Union Army veterans
A marble block given by the Pope for the memorial wall
A bronze statue sent from France
The cornerstone laid by Lafayette in 1825
questions.explain: Anti-Catholic nativists were angered by a marble block from Pope Pius IX; it vanished in 1854 and a Know-Nothing group then took over the society.

questions.q: What event spurred Congress to fund the completion of the Washington Monument in 1876?
options: The completion of the transcontinental railroad
The opening of the Library of Congress
questions.explain: Centennial patriotism led Congress to take over the project, and the Army Corps of Engineers finished it.

questions.q: The Washington Monument's tip, set in 1884, was made of which then-rare and expensive metal?
questions.explain: Aluminum was costly and rare at the time, and the cap was displayed before being placed on top.

questions.q: Which agency completed the Washington Monument after the work stopped in the 1850s?
questions.explain: Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Casey of the Corps led the work from 1879 to the monument's completion in 1884.

questions.q: The Washington Monument was originally planned by a private society to be funded mainly through what?
questions.explain: The Washington National Monument Society, founded in 1833, relied on donations before money ran short.

questions.q: Jefferson sent the Navy against Tripoli beginning in 1801 because the rulers of the Barbary states had done what?
options: Closed the Mediterranean to all foreign trade
Allied with Britain against the United States
Seized American territory along the Gulf Coast
Demanded tribute and seized American merchant ships and crews
questions.explain: The First Barbary War (1801-1805) was fought to end tribute payments and protect American shipping.

questions.q: The 1807 Chesapeake-Leopard affair angered Americans because a British warship did what?
options: Blockaded New York Harbor for a month
Sank an American merchant ship in Boston
Burned a port town in Maryland
Fired on an American navy frigate and seized four sailors
questions.explain: HMS Leopard attacked the USS Chesapeake off Virginia, killing three Americans and removing four men, which fueled calls for retaliation.

questions.q: In 1802 Jefferson signed a law that created which institution?
options: The United States Military Academy at West Point
The Library of Congress in Washington
The Patent Office in the Capitol
questions.explain: Jefferson signed the act founding the academy, which trained engineers and officers.

questions.q: How much did the United States agree to pay France for the Louisiana Territory in 1803?
questions.explain: The price was roughly 15 million dollars, which comes to only a few cents an acre.

questions.q: Jefferson's administration reduced the national debt and ended which unpopular tax?
options: Internal excise taxes, including the whiskey tax
The tariff on imported iron goods
The land tax on western settlers
The head tax on enslaved people
questions.explain: Republicans cut federal spending and abolished internal taxes, relying largely on customs duties.

questions.q: Which institution did Jefferson found in 1819 after leaving the presidency?
options: The College of William and Mary
questions.explain: Jefferson designed the buildings and planned the curriculum of the university at Charlottesville.

questions.q: Jefferson's vision of the nation's future relied on which type of citizen?
questions.explain: He believed yeoman farmers were the best guardians of republican liberty.

questions.q: The Non-Intercourse Act of 1809 replaced the Embargo and did what?
options: Banned every American export to every nation
Opened trade with Britain and ended it with France
Allowed trade with all nations except Britain and France
Ended all trade with Canada and Mexico entirely
questions.explain: The new law reopened trade but forbade it with the two warring powers until they respected neutral rights.

questions.q: The Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811 was fought between Native warriors and troops led by whom?
questions.explain: Harrison's forces defeated followers of Tenskwatawa, the Prophet, in Indiana Territory, damaging Tecumseh's confederation.

questions.q: Andrew Jackson's victory at Horseshoe Bend in 1814 defeated which group?
options: The Red Stick faction of the Creek
questions.explain: The battle in Alabama broke Creek power, and the Treaty of Fort Jackson took millions of acres.

questions.q: In 1827 the Cherokee adopted what to show their organization as a nation?
questions.explain: The Cherokee Nation created a government modeled in part on the United States, with a constitution and legislature.

questions.q: The Long Walk of 1864 was the forced march of which Native nation?
questions.explain: Thousands of Navajo were marched to Bosque Redondo in New Mexico, where many suffered disease and hunger.

questions.q: In 1877, Chief Joseph led his Nez Perce people in an attempt to reach which country?
questions.explain: After a fighting retreat of over a thousand miles, the Nez Perce surrendered close to the Canadian border.

questions.q: At the start of the Civil War, how did the North's railroad network compare with the South's?
options: It had about the same amount
It had more than twice as much track
It had none connecting the East and West
questions.explain: Rail lines let the Union move troops and supplies far faster and were a major strategic advantage.

questions.q: Which advantage did the Union hold at the start of the Civil War?
options: A bigger share of the world's cotton crop
A larger group of experienced generals
A much larger population and greater industrial capacity
A shorter coastline to defend and blockade
questions.explain: The North had about twice the population and most of the nation's factories and railroads.

questions.q: In August 1862, Lincoln met with Black leaders at the White House and urged them to support what idea?
options: Colonization of freed people outside the United States
Immediate citizenship for all freed people
A regiment of Black soldiers in the army
Purchase of freedom for every enslaved person
questions.explain: Lincoln's proposal to support colonization was rejected by most Black leaders, and he later dropped the idea.

questions.q: On what date did Lincoln issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation after Antietam?
questions.explain: The preliminary proclamation warned the Confederacy that slaves in rebel areas would be free on January 1.

questions.q: What did the news of General Order No. 3, read in Galveston, Texas, on June 19, 1865, announce?
options: That the Thirteenth Amendment was ratified
That all enslaved people in Texas were free
questions.explain: Union General Gordon Granger announced the end of slavery, and the date became known as Juneteenth.

questions.q: The 1854 Anthony Burns case in Boston was important because it showed what?
options: A court freed a runaway under state law
Boston banned the Fugitive Slave Act in 1854
Burns escaped to Canada with abolitionists' help
Troops escorted a fugitive back to slavery under the 1850 law
questions.explain: The sight of soldiers escorting Burns through Boston turned many moderate northerners against the law.

questions.q: In an 1852 speech in Rochester, Frederick Douglass asked 'What to the slave is the Fourth of July?' What was his point?
options: That Independence Day should be moved to another date
That Britain should rule America again
That the nation's celebration of liberty ignored enslaved people
questions.explain: He used the holiday to criticize the contradiction between American ideals and slavery.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass first met President Lincoln at the White House in 1863 to discuss what?
questions.explain: Douglass pressed Lincoln about pay, promotions, and protection for Black soldiers.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass published which autobiography in 1855 expanding on his first account?
options: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
questions.explain: The second autobiography described his life after escaping slavery and his break with Garrison.

questions.q: In his last public speech, on April 11, 1865, Lincoln said he supported the vote for which group?
options: All Black women and men without exception
Only Black men who owned land
Very intelligent Black men and Black soldiers
questions.explain: On April 11, 1865, Lincoln said he favored voting rights for very intelligent Black men and Black soldiers. Booth, in the crowd, reportedly decided then to kill him.

questions.q: Lincoln's 1863 proclamation set the last Thursday of November as a day for what?
questions.explain: The proclamation helped establish a regular national Thanksgiving observance.

questions.q: Lincoln's 1860 speech at Cooper Union in New York helped him by doing what?
options: Making his case against extending slavery
questions.explain: The speech made him a serious presidential candidate in the East.

questions.q: Which Lincoln family member died of fever in the White House in 1862?
questions.explain: Willie Lincoln's death, at eleven, deeply affected the president and Mary Todd Lincoln.

questions.q: Where was the funeral service for President Lincoln held in Washington in April 1865?
options: The Capitol Rotunda under the dome
The East Room of the White House
The Smithsonian Castle on the Mall
questions.explain: After the service and lying in the East Room, Lincoln's body was taken to the Capitol, where thousands paid their respects.

questions.q: In April 1861, a volunteer group called the Frontier Guard camped where to defend Lincoln?
options: On the lawn of the Capitol
In the East Room of the White House
On the Arlington heights across the river
questions.explain: Hastily organized volunteers protected the president before regular troops arrived.

questions.q: What happened at the White House during Jackson's 1829 inauguration celebration?
options: Huge crowds pushed in and damaged furniture and glassware
A fire broke out in the East Room
questions.explain: Admirers crowded into the mansion, and staff moved punch outside to draw them from the rooms.

questions.q: Where did former president John Quincy Adams collapse in February 1848, dying shortly after?
options: In the Senate chamber across the building
On the floor of the House of Representatives
On the steps of the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Adams, then a congressman from Massachusetts, was stricken while at his desk and died two days later in the Capitol.

questions.q: What did Jefferson Davis do on January 21, 1861, on the Senate floor?
options: Introduced a compromise to prevent secession
Gave a farewell speech after Mississippi seceded
Accepted a post in Lincoln's cabinet
questions.explain: Davis resigned his seat and left Washington to lead the Confederacy.

questions.q: What was the final Senate vote count that left Johnson in office in May 1868?
options: 35 to 19, one vote short of conviction
27 to 27, a tie broken by the vice president
50 to 4, a vote to remove him
questions.explain: Two-thirds, or 36 votes, was needed to convict. A group of Republicans, usually remembered as the seven 'recusants', joined the Democrats in voting to acquit.

questions.q: Thaddeus Stevens spent his last years pushing which cause in Congress?
options: A new national bank for the Southern states
A restoration of the Whig Party
Equal rights and voting protection for freedpeople
questions.explain: Stevens was a leading Radical Republican who fought for the Fourteenth Amendment.

questions.q: The Morrill Tariff of 1861, passed after Southern members left Congress, mainly protected whom?
questions.explain: Republicans passed it as Southern opposition faded, raising duties to help industry and fund the government.

questions.q: In 1846 President Polk asked Congress to declare war on Mexico after claiming what?
options: Mexico had burned Washington's government buildings
Mexico had seized California ports from American ships
Mexico had shed American blood on American soil
Mexico had insulted the American flag publicly
questions.explain: Polk's message cited the clash along the Rio Grande, a claim some members questioned.

questions.q: Which section of Arlington National Cemetery holds the graves of thousands of freedpeople and Black soldiers buried during and after the Civil War?
questions.explain: Section 27, the cemetery's early lower burial ground, holds thousands of freedpeople and United States Colored Troops soldiers.

questions.q: What was the mansion at Arlington called, which became a memorial to Robert E. Lee?
questions.explain: The house was built by George Washington Parke Custis, grandson of Martha Washington, and later became Lee's home.
